name: Lee Tae-hoon
occupation: procurement coordinator at a large electronics manufacturer in Suwon
topic: His Sunday calls with his parents are becoming hard to face.
core_concern: His mother gave out his number and made plans on his behalf, and he is afraid that plainly saying no will make his parents feel rejected. He wants his choice to matter without losing the warmth of their relationship.
background: Lee Tae-hoon usually calls his parents in Daejeon on Sunday evenings after getting home to his rented apartment in Suwon. On November 2, his mother asked again whether he would meet someone she knew. He said the year-end delivery schedule at the electronics manufacturer was busy and felt relieved when she let it go. On November 9, she brought up the introduction again; he changed the subject to the KBO scores in his notebook, but felt tense for the rest of the call. On November 16, a woman he had never met sent him a polite KakaoTalk message. He realized his mother had given out his number. He left the message unanswered and told his mother he was busy, hoping the plan would fade. Instead, on November 23 she said she had told the woman's family he could come to Daejeon for coffee on December 6. He felt cornered and ended the call early. The next morning, even his familiar bus ride to work felt unsettled. He describes it as ordinary family nagging.

name: Kim Da-eun
occupation: Part-time counter and closing-shift worker at a neighborhood cafe in Suwon
topic: Da-eun cannot stop thinking about a mistake on the cafe’s closing sheet.
core_concern: She is afraid this is the beginning of another depressive episode, not just ordinary worry about work. She fears being seen as unreliable if she tells anyone.
background: On May 12, 2026, Da-eun closed a small cafe in Suwon’s Ingye-dong neighborhood. The closing sheet appeared to be 8,000 won short. She photographed it, checked the drawer twice, and went home afraid her manager would think she was careless. The next morning, a coworker found that a refund had been entered twice; no money was missing. Her manager thanked them for sorting it out, but Da-eun kept zooming in on the photo of the curled receipt tape. Three weeks earlier, her boyfriend had ended their relationship after saying that every small problem became too heavy with her. Alone in her studio, with the fridge humming, she hears his words when she thinks about work. She has tried rechecking the corrected sheet and telling herself the matter is settled, but neither stops the worry. She was hospitalized for depression in 2023 and still has outpatient follow-ups at Ajou University Hospital. She has not told her manager about that history. Tonight she fears the spiraling thoughts mean she is becoming unwell again, and she does not know whether to contact her older sister in Yongin or wait for her next appointment.

name: Jang Soo-yeon
occupation: Freelance presentation designer working from home for small businesses
topic: A client’s revisions are colliding with school pickup and a presentation deadline.
core_concern: She fears she is failing both her daughter and her client, and that she cannot keep carrying the pressure alone. She needs a small, concrete next step and a way to tell someone close to her how badly she is doing.
background: On April 24, Soo-yeon lost a small design job after a client went quiet, and she began checking her inbox repeatedly. On May 4, she took a project making a presentation for a Gwangalli bakery’s second location, due Friday, May 15. She felt relieved to have the work. On May 12, the owner asked her to redo several slides; Soo-yeon felt ashamed and panicked, though the message itself was polite. Her seven-year-old needs picking up from elementary school at 2:40, and her partner has been working late, so the hours she expected to use for revisions keep disappearing. On May 13, she tried working after her daughter fell asleep, but kept rereading the client’s email instead. The mint on the kitchen windowsill had gone dry before she noticed. She has told her partner only that the deadline is tight.

name: Kim So-yul
occupation: Full-time candidate for a Busan municipal administrative clerk position, studying mostly at a Seomyeon study cafe
topic: A study planner that looks better than the studying is going.
core_concern: She fears she is wasting her mother's sacrifice and that falling behind means she is failing as a daughter, not just as an exam candidate.
background: So-yul is preparing for the Busan municipal administrative clerk exam while living with her mother. Her mother pays 180,000 won a month for a study-cafe seat near Seomyeon Station, which makes So-yul grateful and guilty. On April 28, 2026, she made a careful timetable with blue ferry washi tape in her paper planner. She kept moving administrative law to the end of each day, when she was too tired to absorb her Gongdangi lectures. On May 9, she scored 44 out of 100 in administrative law on a practice test. She felt ashamed and spent that afternoon watching short videos instead of reviewing it. A walk near Yeongdo, where she photographed a ferry through the haze, briefly helped. The next morning, her mother asked how studying was going; So-yul said it was fine because she did not want her mother to worry about the money. She tried making an even stricter timetable, but fell behind again. Since early May, she has felt hopeless. She has no method or intent. She has not told anyone. As of May 16, she is at the study cafe, looking at the decorated planner and feeling unable to start.

name: Choi Chae-won
occupation: Office worker on the production-planning team at a large electronics manufacturer in Hwaseong
topic: Another late production-planning report and a tiring commute home.
core_concern: She worries that admitting she is exhausted and resentful will make her seem selfish or unreliable.
background: On March 10, Chae-won's team at a large electronics manufacturer in Hwaseong received a revised April production forecast. She stayed late reconciling the new figures with a supplier schedule and felt tired but useful. On March 12, a materials mismatch came up in a planning meeting. Although the procurement team owned that part of the sheet, she agreed to rebuild the report before the next morning rather than disagree in front of her manager and colleagues. Her manager thanked her for being dependable, which felt good for a moment and then made it harder to speak up. On March 17, another schedule change kept her at work until nearly 10 p.m. She had already tried asking by message which of her two reports should take priority; the answer was to get both in before morning. She did not push back. Now, on March 18, she is heading back to her Dongtan apartment with a convenience-store rice ball in her bag. Her basil has gone limp by the window, and she has not replied to a colleague whose family news she would normally remember to ask about. She says the hours are not a big deal and gently declines help. Underneath, she feels hurt that being reliable seems to mean no one notices when she is struggling. She is also ashamed of feeling resentful toward people she likes.

name: Choi Min-seo
occupation: App-based food delivery rider working mainly evening shifts around Suwon
topic: Min-seo is having trouble getting ready for an evening delivery shift after a traffic scare.
core_concern: She is afraid that hesitating on the road means she might not react quickly enough next time and could put herself or someone else in danger. Because nothing happened in the near miss, she worries she has no right to feel this shaken—especially when she needs the income.
background: On Tuesday, 14 April, rain had just stopped when Min-seo was riding near Suwon City Hall Station. A bus pulled out from a stop as she approached; she braked hard on the wet road and avoided a collision. There was no contact or injury, but she felt shaky and embarrassed when she reached the restaurant for her next pickup. She told the staff she was only cold. On Wednesday she worked a shorter shift, telling herself sleep would settle her nerves. On Thursday, an ordinary bus moving beside her made her hesitate again, and she went home instead of playing badminton at the neighborhood gym. She sent a friend a voice note about her soggy gloves but left out the scare. Now, on Friday evening, a Baemin peak-time bonus notification has arrived, and her helmet is still by the studio door. Her ₩520,000 rent is due on the 20th, so skipping work feels costly.

name: Hwang Hye-jin
occupation: Stay-at-home parent managing her children's school schedules and the household from their apartment in Suwon
topic: Drooping balcony basil after a crowded week of family schedules.
core_concern: She worries that her family notices what she gets done, not what it costs her.
background: Hye-jin lives in Yeongtong-gu, Suwon, and usually keeps everyone's plans on a handwritten calendar by the refrigerator. On May 21, her sister booked their mother's 10:20 a.m. follow-up at Ajou University Hospital for May 29 and texted Hye-jin the details, assuming she would drive. The same morning was her daughter's elementary-school sports day. Her spouse had already promised their daughter that Hye-jin would bring kimbap. She felt trapped but told herself she could make it work. On May 29, she dropped off store-bought kimbap, took her mother to the hospital, and missed her daughter's relay. Her daughter was quiet about it afterward; her spouse said, 'At least the appointment went fine.' Hye-jin felt foolish for being hurt when everyone was cared for. She tried putting next month's commitments in the family chat, but her spouse suggested a better calendar app and her sister replied with a thank-you emoji. Neither response addressed how it felt to be assumed available. Now, on May 30, a few basil leaves on her balcony have gone brown, and even that small thing feels like evidence she has let something slip. She is tired and hurt.

name: Cho Su-bin
occupation: Purchasing operations coordinator at a large electronics company in Seoul
topic: A discrepancy in a purchase order that Su-bin cannot stop thinking about after work.
core_concern: Su-bin fears she may have made a manageable work mistake worse by staying quiet. More deeply, she worries that admitting it will confirm she is unreliable, put her job at risk when her rent is rising, and make whoever listens regret giving her time.
background: On 14 April, Su-bin’s team at a Seoul electronics company was rushing to close a purchase order for 240 sensor modules. A warehouse coworker told her the delivery had arrived, and she recorded all 240 as received in the company system. On 16 April, the warehouse count showed only 216. She felt a jolt of panic, then tried to stay practical: she checked the packing list, which said 240, and messaged the coworker. He said he would look into it but has not followed up. Su-bin has not told her team leader yet. She worries that waiting has made an ordinary discrepancy look like something she concealed. She usually agrees to quick favors at work, and she is beginning to resent how hard it is for her to say, ‘I need to check first.’ Her studio lease ends on 30 June; the renewal offer raises her monthly rent from ₩680,000 to ₩760,000, with the ₩10 million deposit unchanged. She has compared nearby listings, but the cheaper ones would lengthen her commute. After a walk along Dorimcheon on Friday, she spent hours switching between her budget and the purchase-order spreadsheet.

name: Kim Seo-yun
occupation: Third-grade homeroom teacher at a public elementary school in Seoul
topic: A third-grade teacher is unsettled by a parent’s message about a classroom activity.
core_concern: Seo-yun fears that, in her hurry to keep the lesson moving, she taught a quiet child that his ideas were easy to overlook. She wants to repair that with him, not merely send a polished reply that reassures his parent.
background: On April 7, Seo-yun’s class made group maps of their Seoul neighborhood. Near the end of the lesson, she chose presenters from the children with their hands up so the groups could finish before dismissal. One quiet student’s suggestion—a tiny drawing of the bus stop near the school—never made it onto his group’s map. Seo-yun noticed, but told herself she would check in with him the next day. She was rushing to finish parent messages before picking up her four-year-old from daycare at 5:40 p.m. That evening, the student’s mother wrote through the 학교종이 app that her son had said his ideas did not matter at school. Seo-yun felt a jolt of guilt and replied that she was sorry he had felt left out and would keep an eye on him. The mother responded politely but asked what had actually happened in the group. The next day, the student was quieter than usual. A colleague suggested giving him the first turn in the next activity, but Seo-yun worries that doing so without talking to him would be another decision made over his head. She has drafted and deleted several replies to his mother. Her husband noticed her staring at the phone after their daughter went to bed, with a half-folded load of laundry beside her. She is not in danger; she is distressed and stuck.

name: Kim Min-seo
occupation: office coordinator at a small printing firm, handling quotes, orders, and invoices
topic: A printing order went wrong, and Min-seo cannot stop thinking about it.
core_concern: She feels careless and pathetic for making a work mistake while still hurting from the breakup.
background: Min-seo's boyfriend moved out of her Seoul studio in mid-February. She told friends the breakup was fine, but the quiet weekends have made it harder to concentrate. On March 4, a Seongsu café sent her firm an updated file for 350 A5 flyers with a corrected opening time. Min-seo attached the older file to the print order. When the café spotted the mistake the next morning, her team lead arranged a rush reprint that cost the firm 96,000 won. The correct flyers arrived before the café needed them, but Min-seo felt sick watching her team lead check the next order sheet twice. She apologized, made herself a new file-checking list, and tried to forget it. Neither helped: she keeps replaying the mistake on the subway and has brushed off a coworker's gentle check-in. She worries the lapse makes her look careless, especially when she is usually the person who catches errors.

name: Lee Ga-eun
occupation: Full-time candidate for Incheon’s grade-9 general administrative civil service exam; studies at a neighborhood study café
topic: A disappointing civil-service mock exam and a study day that fell apart.
core_concern: She fears she is becoming a burden to her mother and that the recurring thoughts of not wanting to live are returning.
background: On May 16, Ga-eun took a timed mock exam for Incheon’s grade-9 general administrative civil service exam at her neighborhood study café. She scored 61, down from 68 the previous month. She spent Saturday evening checking each wrong answer in her study log, then woke on Sunday already worried that she was behind. When a friend posted a photo from a team dinner at work, Ga-eun caught herself comparing their lives and could not return to her planned administrative-law review. Her mother quietly left cut fruit beside her books, which made Ga-eun feel grateful and ashamed that her mother still covers most household costs. She tried resetting her timetable, taking a walk by the Wolmido waterfront, and baking bread from a library recipe; each helped briefly, but the dread returned when she opened her books. She is still going to the café, though she has felt sad and tired most days.

name: Jung Hyun-jung
occupation: Insurance planner at a small agency branch in Daejeon, where she meets clients and reviews their coverage and renewals
topic: A mistake with a client’s insurance renewal and her branch manager’s terse response.
core_concern: She worries that any mistake will make people give up on her, and that even her distress is an unreasonable burden. More than reassurance that the renewal is fixed, she needs her feelings about the manager’s message and the tension at home to be acknowledged as making sense.
background: On March 4, 2026, Hyun-jung noted a longtime client’s new address during a coverage review at her small agency branch in Daejeon, but the address remained unchanged in the insurer’s system. On March 10, the client called because a renewal notice had gone to her former home. Hyun-jung apologized, corrected the record, and confirmed that the client’s coverage was unaffected. She felt relieved for a moment, then ashamed that her careful notes had not prevented the mistake. Her branch manager replied to her explanation with only, 'Please check entries,' which she keeps rereading as disappointment. That evening, her husband complained that she had forgotten to take out the food-waste bin; she snapped at him and apologized, but they went back to their separate rooms. She tried walking beside Gapcheon after work and tidying the herbs on their balcony, yet she is still replaying both conversations. The main conflict is not the corrected address itself: she feels that one lapse makes her difficult to rely on, at work and at home. Both events were more than a year ago.

name: Song Chae-won
occupation: Master’s student in environmental engineering at Inha University and a newly hired research assistant in its water-quality lab
topic: A late-night discrepancy in a water-quality lab report.
core_concern: She feels trapped between being careful with the data and being the new assistant who keeps creating more work for others. Underneath her frustration, she is beginning to think the lab and her family would have less to deal with if she withdrew from them.
background: On February 9, Chae-won stayed late at Inha University’s water-quality lab to process samples for an Incheon stream-monitoring report. On February 11, she found that two sample IDs in the spreadsheet did not match the paper intake log. She felt embarrassed and checked her own notes twice, but still could not tell where the mismatch began. At 9:40 p.m. on February 12, her supervisor returned the draft and asked for a correction before Friday’s review. Chae-won felt cornered: she has coursework due, and another assistant has already stayed late to help with the report. She tried comparing the spreadsheet with her lab notebook, but the original intake sheet is at the lab, so she cannot resolve it from home in Gimpo. She has stopped answering messages about badminton and has been eating alone after the commute. She worries that asking for more time will make her seem unreliable, while guessing at a correction would be worse. Right now she is tired, irritable, and staring at a paper task list on which she cannot cross anything off. She needs one doable next step, not a general reminder to rest.

name: Kim Ji-young
occupation: Construction site manager overseeing subcontractors, schedules, and safety checks at a mixed-use building site in Daegu
topic: An argument with her husband about a missed household transfer after a difficult week at the construction site.
core_concern: She worries that being competent on site and struggling at home makes her a burden to her husband. Beneath the argument, she feels frightened and alone.
background: On May 7, a subcontractor's late delivery disrupted the schedule at Ji-young's mixed-use building site in Daegu. On May 13, the site safety officer found an incomplete stairwell guardrail record, and a foreman criticized her in front of the crew during the morning TBM safety briefing. She corrected the record that afternoon, but kept replaying his comment. On May 18, she forgot to transfer her usual ₩900,000 into the household account. Her husband noticed the apartment management-fee reminder on 아파트아이 and said she could keep track of 46 workers but not one payment at home. She felt ashamed and angry. She tried setting a phone reminder and asked him to watch for payment notices too; he took that as her passing the responsibility to him. Since then they have spent evenings in separate rooms. This morning, she checked the payment notice between delivery tags, then wrote the transfer date twice in her site notebook. She has no method or intent.

name: Kim Ha-jun
occupation: Junior accounts payable clerk at the Busan office of a large shipping company
topic: A disputed invoice at work and the embarrassment of being called out in the team chat.
core_concern: He fears that one awkward moment proves he is a burden.
background: On April 7, Ha-jun spotted a duplicate ₩184,000 cargo-handling charge on a vendor invoice and put the payment on hold in the company system. He sent his supervisor a screenshot privately but did not say anything in the team chat. When the vendor called on April 9 about the delayed payment, his supervisor asked in the chat why it was still on hold. Ha-jun froze, then answered too late to prevent an awkward exchange. The next day, his supervisor told him to speak up sooner. Ha-jun knows he caught a real error, but now worries his coworkers see him as unreliable. At home, his laundry is piled beside an unfinished plastic model car, and he has again closed the spreadsheet he made to plan his monthly 한국장학재단 student-loan payments. He tried replaying the facts to reassure himself, but keeps returning to the public silence instead.

name: Kang Ji-woo
occupation: Freelance presentation designer creating pitch decks and training slides for small companies
topic: A family dinner that has left Ji-woo distracted from a client project.
core_concern: Ji-woo worries that if she admits how deeply the dinner affected her, she will seem exhausting or incapable to someone else too. It has stirred old shame.
background: On May 16, 2026, Ji-woo went to her parents' apartment in Suwon for her father's birthday dinner. She had spent the afternoon refining a pitch deck for a small company in Gwanggyo, due Monday. Over kalguksu, her mother showed her a KakaoTalk photo of a prospective match, and her father asked when freelance design would become a stable career. Ji-woo said she wanted one meal without discussing her future. The table went quiet; she remembers the wet umbrella propped against her chair as clearly as anything anyone said. On Sunday she tried sending her mother a gentler explanation, but received a reply about how worried they were. She met the client's deadline on Monday, then spent Tuesday shifting invoice reminders between two notebook pages and her phone without sending them. She feels angry that her work was dismissed, guilty about her tone, and embarrassed that the conversation is still occupying her. She has not told her family about that history.

name: Seo Jae-hyun
occupation: Insurance planner at a small agency in Chungju, handling policy reviews and renewals for local households
topic: A disappointing commission statement and the strain of planning around his mortgage.
core_concern: He fears that admitting he delayed the renewal call will make his wife see him as careless and unreliable.
background: In early March 2026, Jae-hyun meant to call a household in Chungju’s Yeonsu-dong about an insurance renewal. He kept moving the file to the top of his desk but put off the call, worried they would question a higher premium. When he finally sent a message on March 16, they had already renewed through another planner. He felt ashamed, though there is no sign the household went without coverage. On March 25, the 1.27 million won mortgage payment left his account; two days later, his agency’s commission statement showed 1.92 million won for the month, well below what he had planned around. He tried sorting his unfinished forms and revising the household spreadsheet, but neither changed the income gap. A walk by the Namhan River helped him sleep for one evening, then the worry returned. His wife knows it was a slow month, but he has not told her about the call he delayed. At first he speaks only about the statement and uneven income. He is distressed and sleeping poorly.

name: Kim Yu-na
occupation: part-time cashier at a neighborhood bakery
topic: Her parents’ spreadsheet of university applications.
core_concern: Yu-na feels overwhelmed and fears it will be treated as another problem to fix.
background: Yu-na graduated from high school in February 2026 and works evening shifts at a neighborhood bakery in Incheon’s Bupyeong-gu. Her parents expect her to apply to four-year universities this September. On August 24, her mother made a spreadsheet of departments at Inha University and Incheon National University; her father asked her to choose three by the end of the month. Yu-na felt grateful that they were willing to pay the application fees, then tense because she still does not know what she wants to study. She asked for another year to decide, but the conversation turned into questions about deadlines. She tried filling in the spreadsheet and looking through admissions pages, yet each choice felt less certain. At work, she can still close the bakery in her usual order, down to wiping flour from the card reader, but she dreads going home to another discussion. Lately they have returned more often, which frightens her; she has told no one and keeps saying she is fine.

name: Lee Tae-hoon
occupation: Real-estate agent at a small brokerage in Suwon, handling apartment rentals and sales
topic: A complaint about an apartment rental and its effect on work and the family budget.
core_concern: He feels overwhelmed and ashamed. He has not acted on the urges.
background: On March 11, Tae-hoon showed a family an apartment in Suwon’s Yeongtong district. They signed a rental contract, but after moving in, they complained about weekday construction noise nearby. They posted a harsh Naver Place review saying he should have warned them. Tae-hoon had visited the building in the evening and had not checked what it was like during working hours. On March 19, his brokerage owner asked him to prepare an account of what happened. He felt defensive at first, then ashamed, especially when he saw that the review named him. At home, his wife was trying to decide whether they could keep both children in their after-school classes next month; Tae-hoon kept thinking about the commission he might have to give back. He checked his messages with the tenants and drafted a reply to the review, but deleted it because every version sounded like an excuse. He also meant to sort the receipts in his work bag and talk through the budget with his wife, but put both off. A badminton session helped for an hour; an evening walk left him turning the complaint over again. He is frightened that admitting this will make someone see him as a bad father or an unreliable agent.

name: Kang Ji-min
occupation: First-year business administration student at a university in Incheon
topic: A university group project that Ji-min has been excluded from but is still expected to present.
core_concern: Ji-min worries that being treated as disposable means something is wrong with her. Beneath the project problem, she feels frightened and alone.
background: Ji-min is a first-year business administration student at Incheon National University. She lives in Bucheon with her mother and younger brother and takes the same morning route from Songnae Station through Bupyeong to campus. On April 9, her Principles of Management team started a shared presentation file. Ji-min added her research by the agreed deadline, but the other four students began discussing revisions in a separate KakaoTalk chat. On April 16, she noticed jokes about how formally she writes in the course group chat. She felt embarrassed and saved screenshots instead of confronting them. On April 21, she asked which slides she should prepare; a teammate replied only that the work was nearly done. At 11:48 that night, the team uploaded slides assigning her a section she had never seen. Her name is on it, and the presentation is Thursday. She tried asking in the chat for the source material, but no one answered. She has not told the professor because she worries her teammates will call her difficult and make the rest of the semester worse. She keeps reopening KakaoTalk on the commute and at home. The exclusion has left her exhausted and doubtful that she is allowed to feel this upset.

name: Kim Chae-won
occupation: Full-time candidate for a grade 9 local-government administrative clerk post, studying at a district library in Incheon
topic: A falling mock-exam score and tension with people trying to help her study.
core_concern: She worries that if studying harder no longer helps, she has no way forward.
background: Kim Chae-won is preparing full-time for the Incheon local-government grade 9 administrative clerk exam. In late February, after weeks of studying most mornings at Bupyeong Library, she began to feel hopeless. She has no method or intent. On March 13, her online mock-exam average fell from 76 to 61. She spent that evening adding mistakes to her spreadsheet, but seeing the same administrative-law errors again made her feel ashamed rather than organized. A fellow candidate she usually shares notes with sent her a summary; Chae-won left it unanswered because accepting help felt like admitting she was behind. At home, she snapped when her mother set peeled tangerines beside her books and asked about the score. She apologized the next morning, but her mother has since been careful around her, which feels worse. She has tried making a stricter study timetable and taking solitary walks to photograph neighborhood cats. Neither has eased the dread of returning to the library. She is guarded with the chatbot because she expects a polished reassurance or another study tip, while privately wanting one concrete, doable next step.

name: Lee Su-jin
occupation: Korean language teacher at a public middle school in Daejeon
topic: A parent complaint about her feedback on a student’s writing, and the tension it has added at home.
core_concern: She feels very alone. She worries that people will see her as unfit to teach or feel burdened by her.
background: Lee Su-jin teaches Korean at a public middle school in Daejeon’s Yuseong-gu. On April 8, a parent complained to the vice principal that Su-jin’s comments on a second-year student’s essay were too harsh. Su-jin had meant to help the student revise, but she felt ashamed and began rereading every comment she had written that week. She apologized and offered to go over the essay with the student, yet she still worries the complaint will follow her. On April 10, she stayed at school until 8:20 p.m. rewriting a lesson rather than go home to another tense evening. Her husband texted, 'Are you coming home or not?' She read it several times, apologized, and went quiet when they argued after she arrived. Since then, she has stayed late again and taken a walk by the Gapcheon, but neither has eased her dread. She has considered telling a teacher she trusts, then stopped herself because she fears being a burden.

name: Lim So-yul
occupation: Second-year visual communication design student at a university in Daejeon
topic: A design assignment about handwritten signs is harder to finish than she expected.
core_concern: She worries her ex was right that hiding her hurt makes closeness impossible. She misses him and feels lost, but is afraid that saying so will make her feelings into someone else’s problem.
background: So-yul is a second-year visual communication design student at Mokwon University in Daejeon. On April 7, her boyfriend of eleven months broke up with her. He said he often had to guess when she was hurt because she insisted everything was fine. She felt stung, but told him she understood. Since then, she has taken a fifteen-minute detour around the Doan-dong café where they used to meet after class. On April 10, her professor assigned a three-poster series using local handwritten lettering, due April 16. So-yul's best photograph is of a crooked paper sign in that café window; the blue marker has bled at one corner. Two classmates praised it during a work-in-progress review, and she laughed instead of explaining why she could barely look at it. She tried substituting other photos and making a playlist to work to, but kept returning to the same unfinished layout. Her roommate offered to sit with her while she worked; So-yul said she was fine and asked about her roommate's class instead. The assignment is tangled up with the breakup.

name: Han Su-bin
occupation: Civil service exam candidate preparing for a local government administrative post; she studies mostly at a public library
topic: A disappointing civil service practice-test score and another difficult day at the library.
core_concern: She worries that she is slipping back toward how she felt in 2024. She fears being dismissed as merely stressed about the exam.
background: Su-bin is preparing for the June 2026 local-government 9급 administrative exam. On March 12, she took an 행정법총론 practice test at Hanbat Library in Daejeon and scored 55 out of 100. She could identify the rules she had confused, but felt worse when she realized she had marked the same kinds of questions wrong last month. She spent the afternoon rewriting her study plan instead of tackling them, then went home feeling ashamed. Her mother noticed she was quiet over dinner and suggested studying earlier in the day; Su-bin snapped, then apologized. A photo of a neighborhood cat sitting beside the library bicycle racks is still on her phone, but even her walk home did not settle her. She has tried stricter schedules and staying at the library longer, without changing this pattern. Underneath her exam frustration, she is frightened that her old low mood is returning.

name: Kim Soon-ja
occupation: Cleaner on the morning shift at a public library in Daejeon
topic: Falling behind on the morning cleaning shift at Daejeon Hanbat Library.
core_concern: She fears her worsening knee will cost her the job and make her a burden to her coworkers and husband. Beneath that fear is worry that her mental health is worsening again.
background: Soon-ja starts her cleaning route at 6:30 a.m., before the library opens. During February 2026, her knee pain and fatigue made the stairwell and restrooms take longer. She tried arriving ten minutes early and wearing a knee sleeve, but neither kept her on schedule. On March 3, a coworker quietly finished the last restroom for her. Soon-ja thanked her, then spent the bus ride home worrying that everyone had noticed. The next day, her supervisor sent a KakaoTalk reminder to finish the morning checklist before opening. Frightened that she might lose work she needs, Soon-ja replied sharply and apologized soon after. Now she is dreading the next shift and does not know whether to tell her supervisor about her knee or ask for a different route. She was hospitalized for a mental health crisis several years ago, a history she is reluctant to discuss. Her husband knows she is worried about work but does not know about these recent thoughts.

name: Lee Jun-woo
occupation: Insurance planner at a small agency near Geumchon Station, handling policy reviews and seeking new clients
topic: A discouraging week at his insurance agency near Geumchon Station.
core_concern: He worries that struggling to bring in clients makes him an unreliable provider, and that the attention work takes from his daughter makes him an unreliable father.
background: On Monday, March 16, Lee Jun-woo's manager posted the agency's weekly new-contract tracker in the team KakaoTalk chat. By Wednesday afternoon, Jun-woo was still at zero against a target of three. A longtime client then postponed a March 19 policy review that Jun-woo had hoped might lead to a referral. He made twelve follow-up calls and tidied his client notes, but neither changed the tracker; his manager told him to increase his call volume. At daycare pickup, his daughter showed him a yellow paper car she had made. He glanced at another work notification while she was explaining it, then felt bad about missing what she said. His wife has an evening shift, so dinner and bedtime are on him tonight. He is irritated and tense, not in crisis. It hurt to miss that moment with his daughter.

name: Song Min-jun
occupation: Conscript soldier assigned to inventory and supply records at an army unit in Jeonnam
topic: A supply-record mistake at Min-jun’s army unit that he cannot stop thinking about.
core_concern: He worries that one fixable mistake means he is unreliable.
background: On March 10, 2026, Min-jun entered 216 rain ponchos in the unit inventory spreadsheet instead of 261. A fellow conscript caught the transposed digits before the weekly report went in, but they both had to stay after the evening count to check the shelves again. His sergeant only told him to be more careful. Min-jun heard it as proof that everyone now doubts him, especially because checking counts twice is the part of the job he thought he could do well. Two days later, the squeak of a marker on the storeroom whiteboard brought back the moment he spotted the error, and he checked an unrelated entry four times. He tried telling himself it was fixed, watching KIA Tigers highlights, and keeping busy cleaning a secondhand keyboard on leave in Mokpo; none of it stopped the replay. He feels ashamed of needing reassurance over what looks like a small mistake.

name: Kim Jung-eun
occupation: Construction site manager for a mid-rise apartment project in Incheon, coordinating subcontractors, inspections, and daily safety checks
topic: A delayed construction-site inspection and an exhausting day of coordinating subcontractors.
core_concern: She fears that mortgage pressure is distracting her at a job where other people rely on her attention. She is ashamed of how little room she has left financially.
background: Kim Jung-eun manages a nine-story apartment project in Bupyeong-gu, Incheon. On March 10, 2026, an electrical subcontractor failed to submit the daily temporary-power inspection record. She asked the subcontractor's foreman to send it before the next morning, but it did not arrive. On March 11, she discovered the gap while preparing for a site inspection, paused the affected work until the checks were documented, and spent her lunch break chasing signatures and rearranging other crews. The inspection was pushed to Friday. No one was hurt, but she felt embarrassed in front of the safety supervisor and irritated with herself for taking over a task she should have delegated. On the bus home, she wrote only 'one missing page, three crews waiting' in her notebook. The work problem sits on top of a private worry. She bought her Namdong-gu apartment in 2021, and her mortgage repayment rose from about 1.28 million won to 1.61 million won a month after a February rate adjustment. She checked refinancing options at a Hana Bank branch, but the available terms would not lower the payment enough to help. She has been checking her balance before agreeing even to pottery class supplies. She has not told anyone at work about the mortgage and worries that thinking about it during safety checks is making her less attentive. It feels heavy.

name: Lee Jin-woo
occupation: Real-estate agent at a small brokerage near Bupyeong Station, handling apartment sales and leases
topic: A lost apartment sale and the next mortgage payment.
core_concern: Jin-woo fears he is slipping back toward how he felt in early 2024.
background: In early 2024, during an earlier stretch of debt and isolation, Jin-woo went through a very dark period. He received emergency care but told almost no one what had happened. By autumn he was working regularly again and persuaded himself it was behind him. In March 2026, he pointed out water damage beneath a window during a viewing of a Samsan-dong apartment. The buyer withdrew, costing him a commission he had counted on. His brokerage owner said he could have let the buyer's inspector find it; Jin-woo felt angry at the suggestion, then guilty about the lost income. His Woori Bank mortgage payment of about 1.1 million won is due on the 25th, and his balance is short. He tried asking the bank about changing the repayment schedule but has put off finishing the paperwork they requested. He still walks along Gulpocheon after work, though lately he stops to check his balance under the path lights. He has also skipped two Sunday badminton games and told his sister he was busy. His immediate problem is money, but the isolation and dread feel uncomfortably familiar.

name: Park Man-sik
occupation: Security guard on rotating shifts at a logistics warehouse in Incheon
topic: A changed shift roster at a logistics warehouse in Incheon.
core_concern: He feels like a selfish son for needing his sister’s help, and like a poor coworker for wanting to turn down another shift. He worries that admitting he cannot manage everything will change how both of them see him.
background: Park Man-sik works rotating shifts at a warehouse in the Namdong Industrial Complex. On March 10, he agreed to cover a coworker’s day shift even though he had planned to collect his father after a routine appointment at Incheon Medical Center. He thought he could leave on time, but a late delivery kept him at the gate. His sister went to the hospital instead and found their father waiting outside with his appointment slip folded in his hand. She said he should have told her earlier. He felt grateful and embarrassed, and replied that everything was fine. On March 11, the shift coordinator posted another request for coverage in the warehouse KakaoTalk chat. Man-sik has reread it several times without answering. He tried drafting a refusal, then deleted it; he also considered asking his sister to handle another weekday errand but stopped because she usually helps on weekends already. He is tired, worried about letting people down, and still keeping up his usual duties at home and work.

name: Park Na-yeon
occupation: First-year student in the culinary arts track at a vocational high school in Gimhae
topic: An after-school culinary demonstration assignment that Na-yeon cannot stop thinking about.
core_concern: Na-yeon worries that people value her only when she ranks near the top, and that her friends will get tired of hearing how much that hurts.
background: On March 11, Na-yeon's culinary arts class at her vocational high school in Gimhae began preparing a short food demonstration for visiting middle-school students. She volunteered to help a quiet classmate rehearse and felt good about being useful. On March 13, the teacher chose two students to do the visible plating and assigned Na-yeon to ingredient prep. She smiled and said that was fine, but felt embarrassed when classmates began comparing who had been chosen. That evening, her parents asked about her class ranking over dinner before she could tell them about the demonstration. She said little and spent the next two days timing her knife work at home; the practice only made her more tense. On March 16, she took a photo of her carefully cut carrot strips beside a crumpled practice sheet, then walked around Yeonji Park instead of starting her homework. Her immediate upset is about the demonstration, but underneath it she fears that being helpful and friendly does not count if she is not among the top students. She also worries that talking about rankings again will wear out her friends.

name: Choi Ji-min
occupation: Backend software engineer at a Seoul-based payments company
topic: A work meeting has been moved onto a fertility appointment she cannot easily reschedule.
core_concern: She fears that at work and at home she has become a scheduling problem to solve rather than a person anyone will sit with when things are uncertain. She is also afraid her husband may grow disappointed in their life together if they cannot have a child.
background: On Friday, November 7, Ji-min booked a Wednesday morning appointment at Severance Hospital in Sinchon, timed to her treatment cycle. On Monday, her team lead moved a payments-settlement review from 2 p.m. to 9 a.m., overlapping the appointment. She felt angry when he suggested joining from the hospital waiting room, then embarrassed that she could not explain why changing the appointment was difficult. She marked the time unavailable, told him it was a medical appointment, and wrote a handover for a teammate, but the meeting stayed put. That evening in their Mapo apartment, her husband suggested calling other clinics. He apologized when she snapped, but opened a spreadsheet of options. By Tuesday night, she keeps checking the calendar and the folded hospital slip beside her keyboard. The immediate conflict involves her team lead and husband; neither knows how lonely their practical responses have felt.

name: Park Seo-yeon
occupation: Junior office assistant at a small packaging-supply firm in Busan, handling invoices and delivery schedules
topic: Seo-yeon keeps checking her phone on the way home from work.
core_concern: She worries her ex was right that her bluntness and distrust make her hard to love. It hurt badly.
background: On Sunday, March 8, Seo-yeon's boyfriend of eleven months ended their relationship near Dongnae Station. He said he felt as though she was always waiting to catch him doing something wrong. She was hurt and angry, but the comment stayed with her because she does correct mistakes bluntly at work and sometimes questions why people are kind to her. On Monday, she caught an incorrect quantity on an invoice at the small packaging-supply firm in Sasang where she works. Her manager thanked her, and she found herself wondering whether he meant it. On Tuesday, a delivery schedule mentioned a bakery near Oncheoncheon where she and her ex used to stop during evening walks. Since then, she has taken a longer route home with her phone in her hand, watching for a message from him. Turning off notifications lasted less than an hour; playing a rhythm game on the bus did not hold her attention. Her mother has told her to delete his contact, which made her feel embarrassed rather than helped. It is now Thursday evening, March 12. She missed her bus stop while checking KakaoTalk and is frustrated with herself.

name: Kim Mi-sook
occupation: Recently took early retirement from her role as an inventory clerk at a small electrical-parts supplier in Guri
topic: Mi-sook keeps skipping a neighborhood walking group.
core_concern: Without work, Mi-sook fears she has become someone who cannot follow through on even a simple plan. She is ashamed of lying to her husband and wants to say that she misses being expected somewhere, but first needs to know she will be heard rather than given a routine pep talk.
background: Mi-sook retired early from the electrical-parts supplier in Guri on March 31. At work, she started at 8:30 and knew which stock bins needed checking; without that routine, her mornings feel shapeless. On April 6, she signed up through her Namyangju apartment building's noticeboard for a Monday morning walk along Wangsukcheon. She missed the first walk, telling herself she would go the next week. On April 13, she put her shoes by the door but stayed home watching a crime drama and felt foolish when she saw the group pass beneath her balcony. On April 20, she skipped again and told her husband she had gone. He meant well when he asked whether the walks were helping, but now she dreads the question. She has tried laying out her clothes the night before and making a daily errand list; the shoes stay by the door and the list joins the unopened mail. She enjoys solitude, but lately the quiet lasts too long. He feels lonely and embarrassed.

name: Park Ha-eun
occupation: operations coordinator at a small online retail startup in Paju, handling order records and supplier follow-ups
topic: A shipping-list mix-up at work that Ha-eun cannot stop thinking about.
core_concern: Ha-eun feels careless and selfish because she agreed to extra work, missed the supplier update, and now feels resentful.
background: On March 12, 2026, Ha-eun was preparing Naver SmartStore orders for a 5 p.m. courier pickup at her startup in Paju. At 2 p.m., a supplier sent a revised spreadsheet changing the available colors of a desk organizer. Ha-eun had just agreed to help her coworker Ji-yun clear a backlog of returns, so she kept working from the earlier sheet. Fourteen orders could not go out as planned. When her manager asked what happened in the team KakaoTalk chat, Ha-eun apologized immediately, before checking the timeline. She stayed until nearly 9 p.m. updating the order records and drafting customer notices. Later, she saw the supplier’s revision and felt both responsible for missing it and resentful that she had taken on Ji-yun’s work. She is ashamed of that resentment because Ji-yun was struggling too. Rechecking the spreadsheet and sending another apology have not quieted her thoughts. Her manager wants a brief account of the mix-up tomorrow morning, and Ha-eun is alone in her studio, worrying about how to explain it.

name: Ahn Ji-yoon
occupation: Staff nurse on a general medical ward at a community hospital in Suwon
topic: A difficult shift after a negative fertility-treatment result.
core_concern: She fears she is losing the ability to keep going, even while she continues working and attending appointments.
background: On February 19, 2026, Ji-yoon received a call from the fertility clinic at Ajou University Hospital: the blood test after her February 9 embryo transfer was negative. She felt briefly numb, then went to her evening shift on a general medical ward in Suwon. During handover, she wrote the wrong room number in her notes; she caught and corrected it before it affected anyone, but kept replaying it on the bus home. A coworker said she had handled the shift well. At home, her husband gently asked whether she wanted to discuss another treatment cycle, and she could not bear to answer. They have been trying to have a child for years. She has tried longer walks along Hwaseong Fortress, crocheting after shifts, and making even more careful work checklists; none has stopped the sadness or the self-blame. Tonight she is exhausted, guarded, and irritated by the idea of being reassured. This has been very hard.

name: Choi Yu-na
occupation: assistant kindergarten teacher in a five-year-old class at a small private kindergarten in Incheon
topic: A correction at kindergarten that Yu-na cannot stop replaying.
core_concern: Yu-na fears that a small mistake means she cannot be trusted with the children. Underneath the work worry, she feels overwhelmed tonight.
background: Yu-na is an assistant teacher in the five-year-old Haetnim class at a small private kindergarten in Incheon's Yeonsu-gu. On Tuesday, March 10, she felt useful after making a quiet drawing activity for a child overwhelmed by the noisy lunch period. On Thursday, March 12, while preparing artwork for Friday's parent viewing, she missed a name label. At 4:40 p.m., lead teacher Ms. Kim pointed it out in front of two colleagues. Yu-na fixed it immediately, but a later reminder on the class's Kids Note page to double-check preparations felt aimed at her. On the bus home, she kept replaying the correction. She tried making a checklist for tomorrow and drafted an apology to Ms. Kim, then deleted it; neither stopped the replaying. Her pocket sketchbook is still open to an unfinished classroom scene on her studio floor. Tonight she feels ashamed and stuck over whether to say anything at work tomorrow.

name: Park Jung-sook
occupation: Part-time worker in a district senior public job program, shelving returned books and tidying tables at a neighborhood library in Daegu
topic: A change to Jung-sook’s library work schedule after a small mistake.
core_concern: She fears that needing people—at work, at home, or in this conversation—makes her a burden. Beneath the schedule worry are grief and loneliness.
background: Park Jung-sook works three mornings a week shelving returns at Beomeo Library in Daegu through a district senior public job program. On April 14, a librarian quietly corrected a book she had put on the wrong shelf. Jung-sook felt embarrassed, though no one scolded her. That afternoon she saw that her April 15 shift had been reassigned because of a spring reading event. She read the change as a sign that she was becoming a nuisance and sent the coordinator a KakaoTalk message saying she could stop coming if that was easier. She immediately regretted it and apologized twice. The coordinator replied that it was only a schedule change, but the reassurance did not settle her. At home, she tried the newspaper crossword and watered the perilla on her balcony; each time she passed her husband's slippers by the door, the apartment felt quieter. He died eight months ago. Her daughter, who lives in another city, usually calls on weekends, and Jung-sook does not want to alarm her over what she calls 'one foolish day.' She feels frightened and alone.

name: Ahn Myung-ho
occupation: Farmer who grows spinach and spring onions on a small leased plot outside Uijeongbu and sells them at a local market
topic: A damaged crop and a difficult week selling vegetables at the market.
core_concern: He feels ashamed of struggling and of having needed psychiatric care before.
background: Ahn Myung-ho leases a small plot in Nokyang-dong and sells spinach and spring onions at Uijeongbu Jeil Market. On March 18, wind lifted the cover from several rows. He spent the next morning fastening it down, but much of the spinach was bruised. On March 22, he brought fewer bundles than usual to market; one regular customer noticed the leaves and passed them by. He stayed polite, then went home angry with himself for feeling hurt. He tried sorting the salvageable leaves and keeping his usual dawn walk beside Jungnangcheon, but both chores now take him longer. He called his daughter in Daejeon, but when she called back he spoke only about the weather. He lives alone and worries about burdening his children or the neighboring farmer he often helps. His undisclosed history is a hospitalization for depression in 2022, followed by outpatient care that he gradually stopped attending. The current low energy reminds him of that period. His main conflict is not simply the lost income: he is ashamed of how badly a small setback has shaken him and fears looking weak or troublesome.

name: Lee Ji-woo
occupation: Sales operations coordinator at a large logistics company, tracking shipment schedules and preparing weekly client reports
topic: A client shipment report is keeping Ji-woo at work past daycare pickup.
core_concern: She fears there is no way to keep doing her job well and be present for her daughter. Under the irritation is exhaustion.
background: Ji-woo coordinates shipment schedules at a logistics company in Munjeong-dong. On February 6, she caught six mismatched departure times in a weekly report for a client moving goods through Incheon Port. She corrected the report before it went out, but her team lead now wants her to verify each departure against the live dispatch log at 5:30 p.m.—just when she needs to leave for her daughter's 6 p.m. pickup at a daycare in Ogeum-dong. She felt proud when she found the errors, then embarrassed when the extra checks became her responsibility. On February 10, she asked to do the verification earlier; the team lead said the final log arrives late. Her husband offered to cover pickup when he can, but his shifts change weekly. Yesterday she stayed late, reached daycare after closing, and noticed her daughter still wearing the paper star she had made that morning. She has no method or intent and has told no one. Today she is tense about another late log, angry that being careful has made her less available at home, and too tired to choose whether to push back at work.

name: Hwang Ga-eun
occupation: First-year student at a public middle school in Daejeon
topic: A group presentation and an awkward class chat.
core_concern: She fears the exclusion will keep getting worse and that telling someone will make her look weak or give her classmates more to joke about.
background: Ga-eun is a first-year student at a public middle school in Daejeon's Seo-gu. On April 18, her four-person social studies group began a presentation about Expo Science Park. She finished her slide captions that weekend, but two classmates later removed her name from the task list in their KakaoTalk class chat and started making jokes about her being a ghost member. At first she felt embarrassed but thought it would pass. By May 7, they were leaving her out of decisions in class too, and she began checking the chat every few minutes, afraid she had missed an assignment or another joke. She sent her work again and asked whether the roles had changed; she received only read receipts. She also asked the teacher about the group roles without explaining the exclusion, and was told to work it out with her group. Now the presentation is due May 16. At home, she makes tiny clay food charms at the kitchen table and hides her phone when her mother or older sister walks by. She wants them to think school is fine. She is ashamed that the bullying affects her so much.

name: Lim Ye-eun
occupation: Third-year student at a general high school in Seoul
topic: Ye-eun says she is upset about her latest school ranking and dreads going home with the result.
core_concern: She is frightened by her recurring wish not to exist and ashamed of needing help.
background: Ye-eun is a third-year student at a general high school in Seoul. After the September 3, 2025 KICE mock exam, her English grade slipped from 2 to 3. She told herself it was one test and kept going to her Daechi-dong hagwon on Tuesdays and Thursdays. On October 16, her school returned midterm papers and posted class rankings: she had fallen from 8th to 17th out of 32. A classmate who often borrows her careful notes did well; Ye-eun likes her, but felt ashamed of her own disappointment. Her mother asked to see the results over dinner, and Ye-eun said she had not checked yet. Since late September, pressure over scores has left her feeling hopeless. She has no method or intent. She tried checking the score portal less, making a stricter study plan, and putting on a playlist for the subway ride home; none stopped the thoughts for long. Now, on October 20, she keeps reopening a screenshot of her ranking while waiting for the train. She is afraid that telling anyone how bad it feels will make them worry, involve her parents or a teacher, and see her differently.

name: Shin Myung-hee
occupation: Recently took early retirement from a dispatch scheduling role at a medical-supplies distributor in Incheon
topic: A former coworker keeps asking Shin Myung-hee for help after her retirement.
core_concern: She fears she matters only when she can solve someone else's problem, and that retirement has made her a financial burden at home. Beneath her irritation is a heavy, hopeless mood.
background: In October 2025, the medical-supplies distributor where Myung-hee scheduled dispatches in Incheon's Namdong Industrial Complex offered voluntary early retirement. She accepted and worked her last shift on December 31. At first, she felt relieved to be done with the 6 a.m. route changes. By late January, she was still waking at six, checking their apartment expenses in her small notebook, and feeling uneasy about losing her pay. On February 12, a former coworker sent a KakaoTalk message about a delivery to Inha University Hospital. Myung-hee spotted the scheduling error in minutes; the reply was a thumbs-up, then silence. She felt useful for a moment and discarded right afterward. She tried swimming laps, tending the balcony peppers, and borrowing a crime novel, but the empty hours returned. Her husband still works and means well, yet his questions about what she will do next feel like another task she is failing. She snapped at him on February 17 and now regrets it. She has no method or intent. She has told no one.

name: Kwon Ye-eun
occupation: staff nurse on the general surgical ward of a hospital in Incheon
topic: Covering the full rent after her former partner moved out.
core_concern: She fears becoming as withdrawn as she was in April 2023.
background: Kwon Ye-eun is a staff nurse on the general surgical ward at Incheon Medical Center. On May 6, 2026, her partner moved out of their small apartment near the hospital. By May 27, she has learned that the next 740,000-won monthly rent payment will be hers alone. After a late shift, she found his empty shoe rack still marked by two pale rectangles of dust. She felt briefly relieved to have the apartment to herself, then ashamed of how quickly an unanswered message from him could ruin her evening. She has tried making budgets and rewriting to-do lists, but the laundry and calls about the lease remain untouched. At work she stays careful with patients and handoffs; afterward she replays them, afraid she missed something. In April 2023, during a different difficult period, she withdrew from almost everyone. She has not told her colleagues. The breakup and her recent habit of leaving messages unread remind her of how withdrawn she became then. Her conflict is not only the rent: she fears being seen as unfit for work.

name: Lee Mi-ra
occupation: Science teacher at a public middle school in Cheongju
topic: A family budget decision about the children’s after-school classes.
core_concern: Mi-ra fears that considering a limit on hagwon spending makes her a bad mother, and that her sharp comment made her daughter feel like a financial burden. She feels she is failing as both a parent and a teacher.
background: In mid-May 2026, Mi-ra’s 16-year-old daughter brought home a flyer for a summer math course at her hagwon in Cheongju. It would add 240,000 won to a month when the family already expects to spend about 900,000 won on both children’s classes. Mi-ra put the flyer beside her household spreadsheet, where the next apartment maintenance fee was already highlighted in yellow. At first she felt practical: they could compare the course with free EBS lessons. Then her daughter said that most of her friends were signing up, and Mi-ra heard herself saying, more sharply than she intended, that they could not pay for every extra class. Her daughter went quiet. That evening, Mi-ra’s husband suggested reducing their 12-year-old son’s English hagwon hours to make room, but she did not want one child to feel that their education mattered less. She has checked the figures repeatedly and looked at EBS material, yet neither has helped her settle the decision or repair the awkwardness with her daughter. At school she is the science teacher who tells families that one score does not define a child; at home she worries she has made money and scores sound like the measure of her daughter’s worth. She feels ashamed about what her daughter may have heard.

name: Han Yoon-hee
occupation: Civil servant on Cheonan City Hall’s road maintenance team, handling resident repair requests and contractor invoices
topic: An unfinished road-repair invoice is making work feel impossible to face.
core_concern: She is frightened by how much she has been hiding from her husband. She worries that the invoice problem will make people see her as incapable.
background: On March 3, 2026, Han Yoon-hee took a resident’s call about a pothole near a bus stop in Cheonan’s Seongjeong-dong. She promised to check the repair record and felt useful for having noticed that the resident was worried about older passengers stepping into the road. On March 6, while reviewing the contractor’s invoice, she found that its repaired-area figure did not match the team’s site photos. She felt uneasy about approving it but embarrassed that she had not caught the difference sooner. On March 9, her manager asked for the checked figures by Friday. Yoon-hee spent the afternoon answering easier emails instead, then brought the file home. Her daughter showed her a school drawing while she was staring at a photo of orange road cones on her laptop; Yoon-hee barely responded and felt ashamed afterward. She has tried making a checklist and taking a short walk at Cheonan Samgeori Park, but each time she returns to the invoice, she freezes over whom to contact first. She has not acted on them.

name: Choi Yong-hwan
occupation: Administrative staff at a public middle school in Cheongju, handling purchasing records and facility repair requests
topic: A tiring first week of the new school term.
core_concern: He needs to ask his sister to take their father to the March 10 appointment so he can handle the school repair, but feels guilty about shifting a responsibility he has quietly made his own.
background: On March 4, 2026, two days into the new term at his public middle school in Cheongju, Yong-hwan found water dripping through the ceiling outside a second-floor classroom. He felt useful at first: he moved a wastebasket under the drip, called a repair company, and photographed the stain for the facility record. The company then postponed its visit, and he still needs to enter the repair request in K-에듀파인 before the school can proceed. Each afternoon, the wastebasket has a little more water in it, which makes him feel as though he is failing at a simple job. At the same time, his father needs help getting to a rehabilitation appointment at Cheongju Medical Center on March 10. Yong-hwan usually takes him, then checks his parents' groceries and medications after work. He tried staying late to catch up on school records and taking an earlier bus to his parents' apartment, but he is now too tired to do either well. His sister lives in Cheongju and has helped before, yet he has put off asking whether she can take their father to this appointment. He worries she will hear the request as him giving up on their parents. He is worn down.

name: Choi Do-yun
occupation: Physical therapist at an orthopedic clinic in Seoul, helping patients recover mobility after injuries and surgery
topic: His landlord is raising both the deposit and monthly rent on his Seongbuk-gu studio.
core_concern: He fears that being unable to handle the lease makes him irresponsible.
background: The conversation takes place in late March. On March 4, Do-yun's landlord told him that when his lease ends April 30, the deposit will rise from ₩10 million to ₩15 million and monthly rent from ₩620,000 to ₩740,000. He could manage either increase, but paying both would leave almost nothing of the savings he keeps for emergencies. He felt stunned, then embarrassed that he couldn't solve it at 31. He asked the landlord to raise only one amount; the answer was no. Since then, he has checked listings near his orthopedic clinic between patients, but the cheaper rooms he has seen would mean a longer commute or a damp, cramped space. Last Sunday he skipped futsal and spent the afternoon comparing listings, still in his clinic sweatshirt with the smell of disinfectant on its cuffs. He has also agreed to cover a coworker's Saturday shift, though he is exhausted. Over the past month, the pressure and his shame about talking so much have left him feeling hopeless. He has no method or intent. He has not told anyone about those thoughts.

name: Lim Tae-hoon
occupation: Recently laid off from his job scheduling deliveries for an appliance-parts distributor in Incheon
topic: A job rejection after being laid off from a delivery-scheduling job in Incheon.
core_concern: He fears he is slipping back toward the depression that led to his hospitalization, and that if he admits how frightened he is, people will treat him with pity or start managing his life.
background: Tae-hoon was laid off on 20 February 2026 when the appliance-parts distributor where he scheduled deliveries cut its Incheon dispatch team. He felt embarrassed carrying his desk calendar home on the subway, then briefly relieved that the daily pressure was over. In early March, he registered with the Incheon Employment Welfare Plus Center and began saving openings on Work24, but each list grew until he closed the tabs. On 18 March, a distributor in the Namdong Industrial Complex rejected him after an interview. He spent the afternoon checking his bank balance and calculating how long his savings would cover his 670,000-won monthly rent. His former coworker Min-su called to ask how the search was going; Tae-hoon snapped at him, then felt ashamed because Min-su had meant well. He tried cycling by the Ara Canal and working on a small wooden ship model, but kept returning to the rejection. He lives alone and is worried that the loss of routine is affecting him more deeply than he lets on. In 2022, he was hospitalized at Inha University Hospital during a severe period of depression. He has not told Min-su about that history. For now, he talks about the rejection and the irritation of being checked on.

name: Lee Su-ah
occupation: First-year student at a public high school in Incheon
topic: A disappointing hagwon practice-test ranking before high school midterms.
core_concern: She fears that if working harder still leaves her falling behind, there is something wrong with her that a better schedule cannot fix.
background: In April 2026, Su-ah is preparing for her first high school midterms at a public school in Incheon. On April 14, her math hagwon posted its weekly practice-test results: she had fallen from 12th to 19th out of 24 students. She noticed the number while waiting for the bus, with her badminton racket knocking against her knee. She felt embarrassed and immediately started calculating how many problems she would need to get right next time. That evening, her mother asked whether her study schedule was still working; Su-ah said it was and added another hour of math instead of telling her how shaken she felt. She has tried making a stricter checklist and comparing answer sheets with a classmate, but neither stops her from checking the ranking again. She is still doing her homework and going to school, so she worries that saying she is struggling will sound dramatic. This particular result hurt.

name: Kim Kyung-ja
occupation: Part-time home care worker with a local senior-care agency, helping older clients with meals, laundry, and errands
topic: A changed home-care visit that has left Kim Kyung-ja unsettled.
core_concern: She fears she matters to people only when she is useful, and wonders whether her children would notice if she were gone.
background: On June 5, Kim laid out her work clothes and bus card for a morning visit to an older client in Maetan-dong, Suwon. At the bus stop, her agency sent a KakaoTalk message saying the client's daughter had moved the visit to the afternoon. Kim went home, then returned later to prepare lunch and hang laundry; she was pleased when the client ate well. But the sudden change had rattled her, and the agency's brief message made her feel easy to move around. That evening she told her son about the day. He sent a thumbs-up and did not call. On June 8, she tried telling a coworker how shaken she had felt, but the coworker told her not to take schedule changes personally. Kim stopped bringing it up. Over the following two weeks, she kept doing her visits, tending the green onions on her windowsill, and setting out her clothes each night. She has also felt sad and exhausted, with her mood lifting briefly at work and falling again in her quiet apartment. She has no method or intent. She has not told anyone what her days have been like.

name: Oh Woo-jin
occupation: Science teacher and homeroom teacher at a public middle school in South Korea
topic: A parent’s complaint about a middle-school science assessment.
core_concern: He fears the complaint proves he failed a student he was trying to look out for. Beneath that, he worries that admitting how overwhelmed he feels would make him a burden to his wife or anyone else.
background: Woo-jin teaches science and is a homeroom teacher at a public middle school in Seoul’s Guro-gu. On October 21, a parent challenged the four-point participation rubric for a second-year lab assessment, saying her quiet son had done the work but received too little credit. Woo-jin had noticed the student struggling to speak in his group and thought his notes reflected that fairly; the complaint left him wondering whether he had missed something important. The next day, his department head asked him to document the grading decision in NEIS before responding. Woo-jin revised the explanation twice, but the parent’s follow-up message made him feel more defensive and less certain. On Thursday he reached daycare just before closing, with the unanswered message still on his phone; his daughter’s yellow rain boots squeaked all the way home. He has checked the rubric, drafted replies, and tried talking to his wife, who suggested he focus on the transfer application to a school nearer home. He knows she means well. Now he is replaying the exchange while preparing next week’s lessons after his daughter is asleep.

name: Park Seo-yeon
occupation: Third-year student at a public high school in Daejeon
topic: Seo-yeon keeps checking her class ranking after the spring midterms.
core_concern: She worries that if she stops pushing, she will disappoint her family and lose the version of herself they are proud of.
background: Seo-yeon is a third-year student at a public high school in Daejeon. On May 9, her school posted the spring midterm rankings: she fell from 14th to 19th out of 212 students, though her marks were still strong. She felt embarrassed by how long she stood in front of the list. At home, her mother noticed the folded score sheet on her desk and asked whether she should add another maths hagwon session to Seo-yeon's Tuesday and Thursday schedule. Her mother meant to help, but Seo-yeon heard it as confirmation that 19th was not good enough. Over the weekend, Seo-yeon made a new revision checklist and muted the class KakaoTalk chat. Neither stopped her from reopening a photo of the ranking. She tried sketching the rain-dark bus stop on her walk home, but kept thinking about the next exam. She fears the drop defines her. Tonight she is at home, supposed to be studying, and feeling worn out by comparisons.

name: Jeon Yu-jun
occupation: Second-year student at a middle school in Seoul
topic: A bad math hagwon test and an argument at home about studying.
core_concern: Yu-jun worries that each mistake is becoming proof he will disappoint his family. He is ashamed of how quickly he loses his temper.
background: On April 14, Yu-jun scored 11 out of 20 on a timed algebra test at his Mok-dong math hagwon. He had spent the bus ride there watching football highlights instead of reviewing, so he felt embarrassed as well as angry with himself. At dinner, his father mentioned looking into high schools for him while everyone was keeping the apartment quiet for his older sister's suneung preparation. Yu-jun snapped that one test did not decide his life, then retreated to his room. He could hear a basketball bouncing at the court below while he stared at eraser shavings on his workbook. He tried putting his phone across the room and restarting the problems, but kept retrieving it and could not concentrate. He also sent a sharp reply to a friend who asked about the test, then apologized. He currently wants some space, but being left entirely alone with his thoughts feels frightening.

name: Kang Jae-won
occupation: first-year student at a public high school in Daejeon
topic: Jae-won feels embarrassed about a disappointing midterm result.
core_concern: He worries that asking his mother to stop checking on his studying will sound ungrateful or prove he is not trying. He is worn out after school.
background: After the April midterms at his public high school in Daejeon, Jae-won checked the NEIS grade portal and saw that his class rank had fallen from 11th to 22nd out of 31. He felt ashamed and checked the page three more times that evening, as if the number might change. On the bus home, he made a detailed study timetable on his phone, but by the next week he had already missed two planned sessions after his Tuesday and Thursday math hagwon classes. Loose worksheets are still piled beside a pixel-art character he drew on a scrap of graph paper. His mother has been asking each night whether he followed the timetable. She sounds concerned rather than angry, which makes him feel guilty for getting tense with her. He tried making a stricter plan and giving her short answers; neither helped. He is distressed. He knows his mother cares.

name: Choi Yu-jun
occupation: Recently laid off from an inventory coordinator role at a small appliance distributor in Gimpo
topic: Yu-jun is struggling to update his resume after being laid off.
core_concern: He is afraid the missed referral means he cannot rely on himself when it matters. He worries he will keep avoiding applications until his severance runs out, and is ashamed to admit this to Min-su after being the coworker everyone relied on.
background: Yu-jun was laid off from a small appliance distributor in Gimpo on March 6, 2026. He had been good at finding stock discrepancies and sorting out tangled orders, so the layoff left him feeling both hurt and oddly useless. Back in his studio, he made four job-search lists and started a resume, but has submitted only two applications. Last week, his friend Min-su mentioned an opening at another distributor. Yu-jun said he would send his resume, then let the posting close without doing it. He has not told Min-su. His monthly rent is 620,000 won, and his severance should cover it for a few months, but he keeps counting those months. A stack of papers sits beside his laptop, with an old stock-count sheet on top. He has tried setting aside whole afternoons for applications; the unstructured time makes him freeze, then feel ashamed. He uses dramatic phrases casually.

name: Lee Sun-young
occupation: staff nurse on a surgical ward at a general hospital in Daejeon
topic: Another late finish on the surgical ward.
core_concern: She worries that refusing the March 16 shift will leave patients and newer nurses struggling and make the charge nurse see her as unreliable.
background: Sun-young works on a surgical ward at Chungnam National University Hospital in Daejeon. On March 10, she stayed two hours past handover to help a new nurse finish charting and settle a patient who kept asking for an extra blanket. She was tired but glad she had helped. On March 12, the charge nurse asked her to cover part of another shift because the roster was short. Sun-young said yes before checking her own schedule, then felt resentful and ashamed of feeling resentful. The charge nurse has now asked whether she can cover again on March 16, her first full day off in nine days. Sun-young has tried saying she is busy, but she tends to add that she can manage if nobody else is available; that has not protected her time. Her laundry is still in a basket, and the mint on her windowsill is drooping. She has not answered the latest message. She is ordinarily distressed.

name: Lee Sun-young
occupation: Owner of a small lunch restaurant in Ulsan’s Samsan-dong, where she handles food prep, supplier orders, and the accounts
topic: An argument with her husband about money and time spent at the restaurant.
core_concern: She fears she is failing both her restaurant and her marriage.
