background: Lee Sun-young runs a small lunch restaurant in Ulsan’s Samsan-dong. On March 17, a slow lunch service made her worry the restaurant was failing, although the week’s sales had been steady. That evening she put off calling her produce supplier about a 740,000-won invoice, then stayed late to prepare side dishes for the next day. Her husband saw the overdue-invoice text when she got home. He said she could not keep working late while avoiding the accounts; she heard it as proof that he thought she was incompetent. She snapped at him, and they spent the evening in separate rooms. She had already tried making an invoice list and asking the supplier for a few extra days, but neither stopped her from falling behind again. She also tried explaining the late prep to her husband by text, which turned into another argument. Since closing on March 18, she has felt ashamed and exhausted.

name: Jang Su-jin
occupation: English instructor for middle-school students at a small hagwon in Suwon
topic: A parent complaint at her Suwon hagwon and the possibility of losing teaching hours.
core_concern: Beneath the worry about her teaching and pay, Su-jin is frightened by her recurring wish not to exist.
background: On March 5, after Su-jin’s first-week English class for new middle-school students, a parent complained to the hagwon director that the reading worksheet was too difficult. Su-jin remembered several students volunteering answers, but she spent that night replaying the one child who had gone quiet. On March 9, the director asked her to rewrite the next two lessons and said her Tuesday and Thursday hours might be reduced in April if the family withdrew. She felt ashamed and frightened about the income: her 16-year-old’s new high-school English hagwon costs 320,000 won a month, and her 13-year-old came home with a 78,000-won list of school supplies and workbooks. She revised the worksheets twice and asked the director for specific feedback, but received only a brief ‘Let’s see how it goes.’ She tried talking to her husband while checking their expenses at the kitchen table; he was tired and suggested waiting until April, which left her feeling alone with the uncertainty. She has no method or intent, and the thought scares her, but she has told no one.

name: Park Ki-hyun
occupation: Owner of a small lunch-and-dinner restaurant in Seoul, where he cooks, orders supplies, and closes up
topic: A slow lunch service and a customer complaint at his Seoul restaurant.
core_concern: He fears that if anyone learns he is struggling with the mortgage, they will see him as an irresponsible owner and a failure.
background: Park Ki-hyun runs a small lunch-and-dinner restaurant in Mangwon-dong and lives in a mortgaged apartment in Eunpyeong-gu. On 10 March 2026, lunch brought in 19 orders instead of the roughly 35 he needs. A customer said the pork was cold; Ki-hyun remade it, but kept replaying the complaint while cleaning to a baseball broadcast. On 11 March, he checked the next day's orders twice before closing and saw that the quieter weeks had left him about 430,000 won short of the 1,460,000 won mortgage payment due to Shinhan Bank on the 25th. He felt ashamed, though he told himself sales might recover. He has already cut ingredient waste by ordering twice a week and used savings to cover last month's gap; neither has solved the problem. His part-time worker noticed him staring at the order sheet, and he brushed it off. He does not want her, his regulars, or his family to know about the mortgage worry. Tonight he is upset.

name: Lim Yoon-hee
occupation: Civil servant handling resident-registration changes at a neighborhood service center in Seoul
topic: A draining day handling resident-registration changes at a Seoul neighborhood service center.
core_concern: She fears she cannot keep up with the mortgage and will lose the home she has worked for.
background: Yoon-hee lives alone in a small apartment in Guro-gu. On February 25, 2026, she saw a Woori Bank notice that her mortgage payment would rise from about 1.16 million to 1.43 million won. She closed the app without opening the full statement. On March 3, the automatic payment fell short by 270,000 won; a bank employee called the next day. She transferred money from her emergency savings to cover it, but she cannot see how to make next month's payment on her civil-service salary. She tried cutting lunches and making a spreadsheet, then stopped when the numbers still did not work. She also asked the bank about changing the payment schedule and came away with forms to submit, not an immediate answer. At work she still catches mistakes in 전입신고 paperwork; this week, the curled receipts from the counter printer and a long queue made her unusually irritable. She felt ashamed that she could sort out residents' records but could not face her own finances. After work, she walked beside Anyangcheon rather than go home to another bank notification. Her underlying fear is losing the apartment and having nobody she can bear telling.

name: Lee Sung-ho
occupation: Sales representative for a medical-supply distributor in Wonju, visiting local clinics to manage orders
topic: A rent increase and a lost clinic account are making it hard for Lee Sung-ho to decide whether to renew his lease.
core_concern: He is afraid that losing income could cost him his home, and that he is less in control than he appears at work.
background: On March 7, his landlord sent a KakaoTalk message saying the monthly rent on his small Myeongnyun-dong apartment would rise from 520,000 to 650,000 won when the lease renews on June 30. Sung-ho felt cornered but told the landlord he expected to stay, then regretted answering so quickly. On March 11, a clinic near Wonju Severance Christian Hospital moved its medical-supply orders to a competitor. He checked his commission figures twice at work, hoping he had misunderstood, and felt ashamed when he had not. That weekend he compared nearby listings, but the deposits and moving costs were more than he has saved. He drafted a message asking the landlord for more time, then deleted it. Now he lies awake revising his budget while a cold cup of pour-over coffee sits on the desk. He feels trapped.

name: Choi Yu-na
occupation: Delivery driver for a Seoul parcel company, handling a regular van route in the city's west
topic: A pile of unsorted delivery receipts in Yu-na’s van.
core_concern: She is afraid she cannot afford to stay near her route after the proposed rent increase, and feels stuck between asking her landlord about it, checking her budget, and viewing another room.
background: Yu-na drives a regular parcel route through Mokdong and Sinjeong from her studio in Guro. On 8 April, her landlord sent a KakaoTalk message proposing that her monthly rent rise from 620000 to 760000 won when her contract renews on 30 June. She felt a jolt of worry but replied that she would think about it. The following Sunday, she tried to work out what she could afford, using pay slips and fuel receipts from the van. She stopped halfway through when she could not find a receipt she needed; a sketch of a faded storefront sign was mixed into the same pile. Since then, she has checked Dabang listings between stops. One cheaper room required a larger deposit, and she has not arranged any viewings. She worries that moving farther away would make her early route harder, while staying might leave too little money each month. She lives alone and has told no one how much the increase worries her. For now, she calls the receipts the problem and turns down help.

name: Kim Ha-eun
occupation: Full-time candidate for Gumi City Hall's grade 9 general administration exam, studying at a neighborhood study café
topic: A study day at the café that felt unproductive.
core_concern: She fears the low score means she may not pass after all this time, and that her family will quietly see her as someone wasting her late twenties. She feels shaken and ashamed after the score.
background: Ha-eun is preparing for the Gumi City Hall grade 9 general administration exam while living off savings and occasional weekend shifts at a stationery shop. On March 14, she scored an average of 58 on a 지방직 9급 mock exam, down from 74 on her previous one. She was disappointed but told herself it was useful practice. The next day, her mother texted to ask how studying was going; Ha-eun replied, 'Fine,' and felt guilty about how long she had been preparing. This week at her Okgyedong study café, she has kept reopening the score page between timed study blocks. Today she spent six hours there, finished only two pages of notes, and let her lunch kimbap go cold. She tried putting her phone in her bag and rewriting her timetable, but neither stopped the checking. She is anxious and frustrated with herself. She calls it a concentration problem.

name: Kim Ji-min
occupation: Office assistant at a small packaging-supply firm in Iksan, handling invoices and delivery calls
topic: An awkward mistake at work that Ji-min keeps replaying.
core_concern: Ji-min fears Hye-jin's brief reply means people are tired of carrying her, and that she has become a burden to everyone.
background: On May 8, Ji-min entered the wrong business registration number for an electronic tax invoice on Hometax for a packaging order from a shop in Iksan's Yeongdeung-dong neighborhood. The order was delivered, but her coworker Hye-jin stayed late with her to cancel and reissue the invoice. Ji-min felt embarrassed, especially when she saw Hye-jin sorting the receipts still piled on Ji-min's desk. On May 12, Ji-min apologized again, and Hye-jin said, 'It's fixed now,' then went back to work. Ji-min cannot tell whether that was reassurance or impatience. She made a color-coded checklist but stopped using it after two days; she also drafted a message asking Hye-jin if things were okay and deleted it. Since her breakup earlier this spring, she has been going home to her studio, leaving messages from friends unanswered, and skipping her usual Baesan Park walks. Her beading tray is still out beside a half-finished phone charm. She worries that needing help at work and needing comfort outside it make her exhausting to be around. She has no one she feels comfortable telling that to directly.

name: Kim Woo-jin
occupation: Conscript soldier handling supply inventory and equipment issue at an army unit in Gyeongnam
topic: A frustrating poncho count at the unit supply room.
core_concern: He worries that one small discrepancy has made him look unreliable to people who depend on him, and he feels ashamed that the pressure made him snap at someone trying to be kind. He feels embarrassed and frustrated.
background: On March 12, 2026, Woo-jin helped issue 32 rain ponchos for a field exercise at his army unit in Gyeongnam. The paper register showed only 31 issued. He first felt embarrassed, then tense as he recounted the stack and checked signatures while the next group waited. A senior corporal pointed out the mismatch in front of the others and told him to fix it before morning. Woo-jin volunteered to handle it, but later found that a returned poncho had been entered under the wrong platoon. Its damp paper tag kept curling off as he tried to match the entries. He has recounted the ponchos three times and shown the likely error to the corporal, but the register cannot be corrected until the other platoon's clerk confirms it tomorrow. Back in the shared barracks, he snapped at a bunkmate who offered to help, then felt bad about it. During phone time he keeps opening NC Dinos highlights without watching them. He is upset, tired, and reluctant to make the incident sound important.

name: Lee Young-ja
occupation: Administrative staff member in the office of a public middle school in Goyang, handling invoices, supply orders, and parent notices
topic: A mistake in a school open-class notice.
core_concern: She is lonely as her divorce is finalized and worries that asking her sister for company will feel like a burden.
background: On May 14, Young-ja sent an e-Alimi notice to about 620 families at her public middle school in Goyang. It gave the wrong arrival time for the May 21 open class. She caught it while checking the printed copy, sent a correction fifteen minutes later, and felt embarrassed when a colleague mentioned the duplicate notifications. She has been distracted since her divorce paperwork moved forward in April. She leaves work promptly to avoid questions, but her small apartment feels especially quiet after dinner; the second chair still has a stack of old parent notices on it. Walks around Ilsan Lake Park and library mysteries help for an hour, not the whole evening. Last week she drafted a text asking her younger sister in Paju to meet for tea, then deleted it because she did not want to impose. The notice mistake is what she will mention first. The harder part is going home with no one to talk to. She wants help choosing one small message she could actually send to her sister.

name: Park Ji-yoon
occupation: Physical therapist at an outpatient orthopedic clinic in Suwon, working mainly with patients recovering from knee and shoulder surgery
topic: Whether to attend her husband’s nephew’s first-birthday party.
core_concern: She fears that the failed cycle makes her a burden or a bad wife.
background: On March 11, Ji-yoon learned that her latest fertility treatment cycle had failed. She cried briefly in the stairwell at her outpatient orthopedic clinic in Suwon, then went back to helping a patient practice stairs after knee surgery. On March 12, her husband’s family added them to the KakaoTalk guest list for his nephew’s doljanchi on Saturday, March 15. Her husband said they could decide later, but she heard disappointment in his voice and apologized. She tried putting her phone away and working on a landscape puzzle; instead, she kept reopening the invitation and the appointment notice for her follow-up at Ajou University Hospital. The party feels unbearable, but declining feels like letting her husband down again. She has felt ashamed and hopeless since the result. She is currently distressed but still going to work and talking with her husband about ordinary plans.

name: Kim Seung-hyun
occupation: Real-estate agent at a small brokerage near Uijeongbu Station, handling apartment and villa leases
topic: A delayed jeonse contract at his brokerage.
core_concern: He worries that wanting evenings to himself makes him a bad son, while continuing to say yes to everything is making him resent his parents.
background: On May 13, a tenant came to the small brokerage near Uijeongbu Station to renew a villa lease with a 170 million won jeonse deposit. The landlord had changed a clause, so Kim Seung-hyun spent the afternoon checking the wording with both sides. He felt useful when the tenant said he had spotted something she would have missed, but he was already late taking groceries to his parents. On May 15, his mother asked him to accompany his father to a routine appointment at Uijeongbu Eulji University Hospital the next morning. Kim explained that the contract needed finishing then and offered to come after work. She said she understood, but called twice the next day while he was with the tenant. He answered sharply on the second call and has felt guilty since. His colleague covered a viewing so he could visit his parents that evening; the visit was polite, but he stayed longer than he wanted. He has tried keeping their appointments in his phone and arranging errands ahead of time, yet any free evening still seems to fill up. Now the contract is nearly settled, but he is tired and irritable. He wants a quiet evening.

name: Jung Su-bin
occupation: Junior accounts assistant at a six-person office-supply distributor in Seoul
topic: An invoice correction at work that Su-bin keeps putting off.
core_concern: She is frightened by her recent wishes not to exist and worries that admitting them will make her seem dramatic or incapable of handling work.
background: On April 9, Su-bin noticed she had entered the wrong unit price on an invoice for a regular customer. She usually catches other people's mistakes, so she felt especially ashamed. Her manager at the six-person office-supply distributor told her to prepare a corrected tax invoice in Hometax. She opened the form twice but closed it each time, afraid she would make another mistake. On April 11, she bought a used mystery-novel set online to distract herself, then saw her bank balance and tried to cancel it. At home, her Korea Student Aid Foundation loan paperwork is still unopened. Her mother has noticed she is quiet, but Su-bin has said only that work is busy. Right now she is at home, looking at the unfinished correction on her laptop.

name: Lee Seung-min
occupation: Full-time candidate for the Gyeonggi Province grade-nine general administration civil service exam, studying most weekdays at a public library in Yongin
topic: A falling civil-service mock-exam score and tension at home.
core_concern: He fears that repeated poor scores mean he is wasting his parents' support and that his life has narrowed to failing at the library and being difficult at home. He wants those feelings acknowledged as making sense, and he is carrying passive wishes not to exist.
background: Lee studies most weekdays at Yongin Jungang Library for the Gyeonggi Province grade-nine general administration exam. His average on a Gongdangi mock exam fell from 72 in February to 64 on March 14. He spent the next morning rewriting his study timetable instead of starting an administrative-law practice set, then felt angry with himself for losing another hour. At dinner, his mother asked whether he should also apply for office jobs; he snapped at her and later felt guilty. He has tried tracking mistakes by subject and taking short rides along the Tancheon trail, but lately neither has quieted the thought that he is falling behind while living off his parents. He has no method or intent. Right now he is guarded and irritable; the score, the wasted study time, and the guilt at home hurt.

name: Lee Eun-sook
occupation: Retired circulation clerk at a public library in Daegu
topic: A duplicate message in a library volunteer KakaoTalk chat.
core_concern: She worries that one awkward message means she is too unsure of herself to be useful at the library, and that she is becoming someone her husband must manage. She wants help choosing one doable step toward Saturday’s shift.
background: On Tuesday, 14 April, Eun-sook signed up for a 90-minute Saturday morning volunteer shift at Daegu Metropolitan Suseong Library. She hoped it would give her somewhere to go and a small responsibility again, two years after retiring from circulation work. On Thursday, while confirming the time in the volunteers’ KakaoTalk room, she accidentally sent the same message twice. The coordinator, Ms. Park, replied with a thumbs-up. Eun-sook felt embarrassed, then spent the afternoon rereading the chat and worrying that she had made a poor first impression. She asked her husband whether she should cancel; he offered to contact the library for her, which left her feeling more dependent on him. She has tried distracting herself with her balcony plants, but keeps checking her phone. Beneath the small mistake, she fears she may no longer be capable of being useful to other people.

name: Kim Seo-yeon
occupation: Third-year student at a public middle school in Mapo-gu, Seoul
topic: A blank high-school preference survey and constant talk about scores at home.
core_concern: The pressure has left her feeling hopeless.
background: On November 17, 2025, Seo-yeon's homeroom teacher reminded her to return a preliminary high-school preference survey. She had left it blank since late October. At first she felt merely behind; after her older sister took the suneung on November 13, dinner conversations turned to Seo-yeon's grades and which high school she might attend. She now feels trapped whenever someone asks what she wants. On the bus home through Mapo-gu, she made a playlist and sketched the sign of a small stationery shop, but neither held her attention for long. She tried telling her mother that the school talk was exhausting; her mother replied that planning early would make things easier. Seo-yeon stopped trying to explain. She has received mental-health care since 2024. She is frightened by those thoughts and unsure whether saying them aloud will lead to being scolded or dismissed. She starts at an emotional level of 35 out of 100.

name: Lee Na-yeon
occupation: Full-time candidate for the local government grade 9 general administration exam; studies at an Incheon public library
topic: A disappointing civil-service mock exam and another evening of studying alone.
core_concern: She fears that struggling again, given her psychiatric history, makes her weak, disappointing, or a burden. She was hospitalized for depression before and is afraid her family will think she has failed again.
background: Na-yeon is preparing for the local government grade 9 general administration exam at Incheon Metropolitan City Michuhol Library. On May 16, she scored 61 in administrative law on an online mock exam, despite having spent the week reviewing that subject. She felt embarrassed, then stayed until closing to copy small mistakes into her notebook, calling the whole day wasted. At dinner, her mother asked how studying went; Na-yeon said it was fine and helped her younger brother find a missing school worksheet instead. Later she watched KBO highlights with the sound off but could not follow the game. A waterfront walk and rewriting tomorrow's schedule did not settle her thoughts. In 2023, she was hospitalized during an episode of depression. Her mother knows about that time, but Na-yeon has not told her how hopeless and withdrawn she feels lately. She worries that needing help again would make her family see her as weak or burdensome. She is back at the library, following her schedule, but avoiding messages from home.

name: Lee Seo-jun
occupation: Part-time closing-shift barista at a neighborhood cafe in Daejeon
topic: Seo-jun keeps checking his phone during closing shifts at the cafe.
core_concern: He is afraid that replying to Ji-eun about her belongings will expose how much he still wants to talk to her. He wants help choosing one small, neutral next step—probably a short KakaoTalk reply—but is wary of advice that makes it sound easy.
background: Seo-jun and his girlfriend, Ji-eun, broke up on April 12 after an argument about how often his closing shifts disrupted their plans. He felt hurt and defensive, but they ended the conversation without shouting. On April 19, she sent a KakaoTalk message asking when she could collect a canvas tote and a blue pasta bowl from his studio in Tanbang-dong. He felt a rush of hope at seeing her name, then embarrassed that a practical message affected him so much. He typed three replies and deleted them because each sounded either cold or like an excuse to keep talking. Since then, he has checked his phone between wiping down the espresso machine and counting the till, though he still closes the cafe properly at 10:30 p.m. On his walk by the Gapcheon, he decided he should answer, but went home and left the tote by the door instead. He wants to return her things without turning the exchange into another conversation about the breakup.

name: Kim Jung-sook
occupation: Civil servant at Chuncheon City Hall, where she reviews small-business permit applications
topic: A difficult small-business permit application at Chuncheon City Hall.
core_concern: She fears her mother has begun keeping problems from her because of her sharp tone. She is ashamed of snapping at her and worries that trying to manage every detail is making her someone her mother cannot comfortably turn to.
background: On 9 June, Jung-sook noticed that the floor area on a new Myeong-dong noodle shop’s drawing did not match its application. Her supervisor wanted the file cleared before closing, and the applicant had already waited at the counter for forty minutes. She felt pressured, then embarrassed when her correction came out sharper than she intended. That evening, while dropping groceries at her parents’ apartment, she found that her mother was confused about the date of a clinic visit. Jung-sook snapped, asking whether she had to remember everything for everyone. Her mother went quiet and said she would not bother her next time. Jung-sook apologized the following morning, but her mother still seemed reluctant to tell her what was going on. A phone reminder and a new appointment list have not eased Jung-sook’s worry. She starts the conversation talking only about the permit.

name: Han Eun-jung
occupation: Fifth-grade homeroom teacher at a public elementary school in Gimpo
topic: Staying late at school and still feeling behind.
core_concern: She worries that she is sinking back into a very low mood.
background: Eun-jung teaches a fifth-grade class of 28 at a public elementary school in Gimpo. Since the new term began in March, parent messages on Hi-Class and paperwork in NEIS have filled the time after dismissal. On March 11, she stayed late to finish consent forms for an April field trip, then noticed a quiet student had waited all day to talk to her. She made time for the student and felt glad she had, but went home with the forms unfinished. The following week she made a detailed catch-up schedule; two parent calls disrupted it, and she missed her usual walk along the Gimpo Hangang canal. Last Thursday she left school after 7 p.m. and found her daughter’s hagwon dinner still in its wrapper on the kitchen table. She felt guilty and oddly numb. Her husband has suggested a stricter system, but another plan feels like one more thing she could fail at. She has no method or intent. She is afraid that saying any of this aloud will alarm her family and lead to more demands.

name: Lee Ye-eun
occupation: Factory worker at an Incheon electronics plant, inspecting and packing assembled power adapters
topic: Ye-eun keeps putting off laundry and feels bad about canceling plans with a friend.
core_concern: She worries that being unable to manage ordinary life outside the factory means she is letting everyone down. She is also carrying a heavy, hopeless mood.
background: Ye-eun works inspecting and packing power adapters at a plant in Incheon's Namdong Industrial Complex. Since March 11, her line has run late several nights a week, sometimes keeping her there until 9:30 p.m. She still checks each adapter carefully and has not missed a shift, but she gets home too tired to do much. On March 22, she promised her friend Min-seo a beaded phone charm and agreed to meet her after work the following Saturday. She was looking forward to it, then left the charm unfinished and waited until the last minute to cancel. Min-seo replied kindly, which made Ye-eun feel worse rather than relieved. She tried setting a laundry reminder and laying out her work clothes the night before, but now a bag of clothes sits by her studio door while she buys another clean pair of socks at the convenience store. Over the past month, on some evenings after work, she has felt hopeless. She has no method or intent. She doesn't want anyone to make a fuss. Beneath her casual complaint, she hopes someone will notice how worn down she is without pushing her to fix everything at once.

name: Kim Ha-jun
occupation: Homeroom teacher for five-year-olds at a small kindergarten in Daejeon
topic: Staying late to prepare a kindergarten activity.
core_concern: He worries the parent was right: that in a moment when a child needed him, he failed to notice quickly enough. He is afraid this says something about whether he is good at caring for his class, not just whether he handled one afternoon badly. The parent’s message is what he cannot stop thinking about.
background: Ha-jun teaches a five-year-old class at a small kindergarten in Daejeon’s Seo-gu. On March 10, a child’s paper flower tore during a busy afternoon activity. Ha-jun saw the child crying, but he was helping two other children and did not check in until a few minutes later. That evening, the child’s parent wrote through Kids Note that their child had felt ignored. Ha-jun felt embarrassed and uneasy. The next morning, the director asked him to reply; he apologized and explained what had happened. The parent answered, 'Please pay closer attention.' Since then, he has kept the classroom routine steady, but he replays those few minutes on the bus home. The child seemed cheerful the next day, yet that has not settled his worry. He tried going bouldering and telling himself it was nothing; neither stopped the replaying. Tonight he stayed late cutting paper petals for tomorrow’s activity, then brought the unfinished stack to his studio.

name: Kim Na-yeon
occupation: Staff nurse on a surgical ward at a general hospital in Iksan
topic: Taking extra weekend shifts on the surgical ward.
core_concern: She fears that being alone after the breakup is pulling her back toward the withdrawn state she remembers from a dark period years ago.
background: Na-yeon's boyfriend ended their two-year relationship on February 2, 2026. She told him she would be fine, then began filling her weekends with errands and extra shifts. On March 12, when the surgical ward's KakaoTalk group asked for someone to cover Saturday evening at Wonkwang University Hospital, she volunteered immediately. She felt relieved to have a plan, then embarrassed when a colleague casually asked whether her boyfriend would still pick her up afterward. At home, she left her phone face down beside an unfinished miniature room kit and couldn't settle into the quiet. She has tried walking at Baesan Park and keeping busy, but neither has made the weekends feel less lonely. Between 2021 and 2023, she went through a long, dark period. She has not told her colleagues or former boyfriend about that history. The familiar impulse to withdraw worries her. The quiet has become very hard.

name: Han Yu-na
occupation: Freelance graphic designer creating menus, packaging, and social media graphics for small businesses
topic: A last-minute packaging revision for a Seongsu café.
core_concern: Yu-na fears looking unreliable or unstable for feeling overwhelmed. The revision has brought back memories of her past hospitalization, which she is reluctant to mention.
background: On March 12, Yu-na sent the final design for a Seongsu café’s madeleine sleeves to a printer in Euljiro. The next morning, the café owner asked her to change the allergen text and have a new proof ready by Monday, March 16. Yu-na wants to keep the client, but the printer needs the revised file sooner than she can comfortably promise. She has checked the text against the owner’s message, made two versions, and drafted a reply explaining the timing; she keeps deleting the reply before sending it. The café’s 380,000-won balance is due after delivery, and she has a Korea Student Aid Foundation loan payment later this month. A blue ink smudge on her sketchbook has become a small reminder of how long she has sat at the same desk. In 2023, she was hospitalized during a severe depressive episode; she still attends outpatient psychiatric appointments. This setback has stirred up memories of that period. She feels embarrassed that a routine client request has affected her so much, and fears someone will see her as unreliable or unstable if she says she needs more time.

name: Kim Su-bin
occupation: Job seeker applying for entry-level inventory clerk roles at distribution centers near Incheon
topic: A résumé mistake and a rejection from an inventory clerk job.
core_concern: She is afraid that one small mistake proves she will never catch up.
background: Su-bin tracks every application in a spreadsheet. On the 6th of this month, she applied through Saramin to two entry-level inventory clerk jobs at distribution centers near Incheon's Namdong Industrial Complex. On the 9th, she noticed that her résumé listed her graduation year as 2023 instead of 2024. She corrected the profile and sent both employers a short follow-up, but felt embarrassed that they had seen the mistake. One sent a standard rejection on the 12th; the other has not replied. She cannot know whether the typo mattered, but keeps rereading the rejection as proof she is falling behind. Her mother has been asking whether any employers have called, and Su-bin has started leaving those messages unanswered for a few hours when she panics. Yesterday she took a walk near Juan Station and photographed a cat beside a convenience-store crate; she felt better briefly, then began worrying again at home. She has no method or intent.

name: Kang Ye-eun
occupation: Full-time candidate for a local-government administrative civil service position, studying most weekdays at a study café in Ansan
topic: A disappointing civil-service mock exam and a difficult week at the study café.
core_concern: She fears she may not pass, cannot afford to keep preparing indefinitely, and has become a burden to her mother. She feels trapped between continuing and quitting.
background: Ye-eun is preparing for the June local-government administrative civil-service exam. On Saturday, March 14, she scored 63 on a mock exam after scoring 74 the previous month. She spent Sunday rechecking questions she already understood, then fell behind the schedule taped inside her notebook. By Wednesday, she was still going to her study café in Jungang-dong but barely speaking to the regulars. Her mother, trying to be practical rather than critical, mentioned a short-term office opening at Ansan City Hall over dinner. Ye-eun heard it as a sign that her mother was tired of supporting her. She tried making a stricter timetable and taking an evening walk around Ansan Lake Park, but neither settled the thought that preparing is costing the household time and money with no clear end. She has answered a friend's messages with jokes instead of saying how stuck she feels. Tonight she came home with her practice papers still in her bag; her mother left sliced pear on the kitchen table, which made her feel cared for and guilty at once.

name: Park Min-seo
occupation: Job seeker applying for junior purchasing and inventory roles at distribution companies near Namyangju
topic: A job application deadline and a confusing set of résumé files.
core_concern: She worries that her disorganized applications mean she cannot manage her own job search, and she is ashamed to say she needs encouragement. What she most wants is one concrete, doable next step toward submitting this application.
background: On June 12, Min-seo received a rejection from a Guri wholesaler; she spent the afternoon wondering whether she had sent the wrong résumé version. The next day, she found a Saramin posting for a junior purchasing and inventory role at a distributor in Namyangju’s Jinjeop-eup. It closes at 6 p.m. on June 18. She liked that the work involved tracking stock, something she had done at a neighborhood stationery shop, but the required personal statement stopped her. On June 14, she renamed three résumé files and copied an old statement into a new document. She still could not tell which file she had sent to which employer, and the new document remains mostly blank. On June 15, her mother asked about the search while putting away side dishes after dinner. Min-seo said it was going fine, then stayed up looking at the open application tab. She feels embarrassed by the delay and worries her mother will see it as laziness. Now, on June 16, she is frustrated rather than in crisis.

name: Lee Ji-min
occupation: Job seeker applying for junior inventory coordinator roles at Seoul online retailers, after a fixed-term stock records job ended
topic: A rejection from a junior inventory coordinator job at a Seoul online retailer.
core_concern: The rejection has left her frightened and alone, and today feels harder than usual.
background: Ji-min’s fixed-term stock-records job at a Guro logistics center ended on April 30. She has logged 31 applications since early April and has savings for her share of the apartment rent through July. On May 14, she interviewed for a junior inventory coordinator role at 29CM and came home hopeful because she could answer a question about mismatched SKU counts. On May 20, a brief rejection email arrived while she was eating breakfast; she entered it in her spreadsheet, then could not bear to look at the remaining applications. She tried walking along Anyangcheon and photographing the yellow flowers by the path, but kept replaying the interview instead. Her cousin, who shares the apartment, noticed she had barely eaten and offered to help with applications. Ji-min said she was fine. She is frightened. She was hospitalized during a mental-health crisis in 2023 and still attends outpatient appointments. She worries that telling her cousin how she feels will turn her into a problem to manage.

name: Lee Ji-woo
occupation: Full-time candidate for Jeju's ninth-grade general administrative civil service exam, studying at a neighborhood library
topic: A disappointing civil service practice-exam score and an awkward evening at home.
core_concern: She worries that her mother thinks she is lazy and ungrateful because she played a phone game, fell behind her own plan, and snapped despite her mother's quiet care.
background: Ji-woo is preparing for Jeju's ninth-grade general administrative civil service exam at Tamna Library in Jeju City. On March 11, she scored an average of 68 on a timed five-subject practice exam, despite having made a detailed revision plan the week before. She remembered several questions afterward but had mixed up two administrative law concepts under time pressure, which made her feel frustrated. That afternoon, she avoided sorting her notes and played a rhythm game on her phone for forty minutes. Guilty about it, she stayed up past 2 a.m. trying to catch up. On March 12, her mother asked how studying had gone while Ji-woo was helping cut spring onions for dinner. Ji-woo snapped that she didn't want to talk about scores, then retreated to her room. Her mother later left a peeled tangerine outside the door. Ji-woo has tried making stricter timetables and studying later after setbacks, but both leave her more overwhelmed. Tonight she is upset about the score and ashamed of snapping at her mother.

name: Han Ji-ho
occupation: Conscript soldier assigned to inventory and equipment records in a South Korean Army battalion supply office
topic: A supply-office inventory count that does not match the records.
core_concern: Ji-ho is afraid that being honest about the mismatch will let his corporal down or unfairly implicate another soldier, but he cannot bring himself to sign a count he knows is wrong.
background: On April 14, Ji-ho counted 30 rain ponchos in his battalion supply room, though the ledger showed 32. Two had been signed out for field training on April 12, but he could not find return slips. He felt uneasy rather than panicked and checked the shelves again, getting dust on the edge of his pocket notebook. On April 15, he asked the soldiers who handled the returns; neither remembered taking the ponchos back. His corporal, busy preparing for an April 17 inspection, told him to use the previous count. Ji-ho did not want to accuse anyone without evidence, but signing off on 32 felt dishonest. He stayed late comparing issue records and still found nothing. Now, during permitted phone time in the barracks, he is worn down and worried that raising the discrepancy will disappoint his corporal or put another soldier under suspicion.

name: Kang Su-jin
occupation: Stay-at-home parent and primary caregiver for her eight-year-old daughter; she also does part-time invoice entry from home for a small wholesaler whose staffing shortage has pushed her hours well beyond what she agreed to.
topic: A late invoice-entry deadline collides with school pickup and evening childcare.
core_concern: Su-jin fears that if she stops answering her manager or her husband, they will take her silence as proof that she is unreliable. What she most needs right now is a little space before deciding whether and how to reply.
background: On Tuesday, March 24, Su-jin's manager at a small Daejeon wholesaler sent a KakaoTalk message at 2:20 p.m. asking her to check 62 purchase slips before the next morning's accounting handoff. She had agreed to roughly three hours of invoice entry a week, but worked twelve hours last week because of a staffing shortage. At first she felt annoyed, then guilty for feeling annoyed. She replied that she would look after school pickup. Her daughter's taekwondo hagwon shuttle was due at 5:00, and her husband was commuting home from Cheongju, so dinner and the evening routine remained hers. At 7:15, the manager asked her to confirm whether the slips would be done tonight. Su-jin drafted a reply offering tomorrow morning, deleted it, and set her phone face down beside a cup of cold barley tea. A previous attempt to explain the extra hours had received only 'We're all busy right now.' Her husband has suggested simply saying no, which felt like another demand rather than help. It is now just after 9 p.m.; her daughter is getting ready for bed, the slips are unopened, and each KakaoTalk alert makes Su-jin tense.

name: Lee Su-jin
occupation: Insurance planner at a Daejeon branch office, managing existing clients' policies and renewals
topic: Her mother went to a hospital checkup without her.
core_concern: She worries that wanting an evening without caregiving makes her a bad daughter, even though her parents are capable of doing some things on their own.
background: On April 15, Su-jin was at the Daejeon branch finishing three clients’ policy renewals when her mother, 73, took the 604 bus alone to a 9:40 a.m. ophthalmology follow-up at Daejeon St. Mary’s Hospital. Su-jin had offered to accompany her, but her mother said she could manage. At work, Su-jin felt relieved to have the morning free; when her mother later texted that the visit went fine, the relief turned to guilt. She stopped by her parents’ apartment that evening with groceries and found the hospital receipt neatly tucked under a magnet on the refrigerator. Her father said they did not need her to come over every night. She smiled and said she knew, then went home feeling both grateful and strangely unwanted. She has tried making a shared appointment calendar and setting aside one evening a week for herself, but she checks for missed calls and often visits anyway. She is tired and persistently sad. She was relieved not to go and now feels guilty for wanting time to herself.

name: Lee Ji-hoon
occupation: Civil service exam candidate preparing for a local government administrative post in Daejeon
topic: A disappointing civil-service mock exam and a Sunday call he does not want to answer.
core_concern: He feels fear and shame about the score. He is also afraid that he is slipping back into a time he thought was behind him, and that saying so will make him a burden.
background: Ji-hoon is preparing for the Daejeon Metropolitan City local-government grade-9 administrative exam. On Saturday, March 14, 2026, he took a timed mock exam at his Dunsan-dong hagwon and scored 61, down from 73 the previous week. He had followed his study schedule closely, so the drop frightened him more than the number itself. On the bus home, he kept looking at a red correction mark on the corner of his answer sheet. He spent that evening rebuilding his wrong-answer notebook, but on Sunday he could not bring himself to open it. His mother called at their usual time; he watched the phone ring and then felt guilty for avoiding her. A walk by the Gapcheon stream and an attempt to redraw his weekly planner helped briefly, but he returned to the same thought: if one bad test can stop him working, perhaps he cannot be trusted to keep going until the exam. He has not told his parents or fellow candidates. Right now he is subdued rather than visibly panicked, at about 35 out of 100.

name: Lee Hee-jung
occupation: Production planning manager at an auto-parts supplier in Asan, supervising a small scheduling team
topic: A last-minute delivery schedule change at the auto-parts supplier.
core_concern: She feels upset and overextended, even though she volunteered to cover the work. She fears that asking for help would mean failing people who count on her.
background: On March 18, 2026, Hee-jung had nearly finished the next morning's delivery schedule for the Hyundai Motor Asan Plant when a customer order revision arrived at 4 p.m. A scheduler on her small team also had to leave early for a sick child. Hee-jung said she would cover the changes, as she usually does, but felt her stomach sink when she remembered that her mother has a 9:30 a.m. appointment at Soonchunhyang University Cheonan Hospital on March 19. Hee-jung had promised to drive her and check the medication list with her father tonight. Her younger brother in Cheonan cannot take the morning off. She tried reshuffling the delivery slots and phoning him again, but neither solved the overlap. A paper bag of groceries for her parents is still on her passenger seat. She is irritated by the schedule change, ashamed that she wants someone else to take over, and worried that she cannot manage both and will disappoint her team and her parents.

name: Seo Mi-young
occupation: backend software engineer at a Seoul online grocery company
topic: A late-night production incident at her online grocery company.
core_concern: She worries people value her only when she fixes things, and that needing care herself will make her seem difficult.
background: On Tuesday, March 17, a change to the delivery-slot API caused some Seoul customers to see unavailable slots as open just before the 11 p.m. next-day delivery cutoff. Mi-young traced the bug while the on-call chat filled with alerts. She felt relieved when her patch worked, then ashamed after noticing a sharp reply she had sent to a teammate who asked for an update. She apologized in KakaoWork the next morning, but the teammate has not replied. Her manager thanked her for the fix and asked her to take an extra on-call shift this weekend; she agreed before thinking. She tried making a checklist to settle her nerves, but keeps reopening the incident log and replaying her message. She is now at her desk with cold convenience-store kimbap beside her, tired and unable to leave work behind. She feels worn down.

name: Lim Ji-yoon
occupation: Job seeker applying for entry-level inventory coordinator roles at online retailers in Seoul
topic: An uncertain inventory coordinator application and an email she regrets sending.
core_concern: She has felt low on and off for a long time. The job search has made her feel trapped and burdensome.
background: Ji-yoon has applied for 34 entry-level inventory roles since January, tracking each one in a spreadsheet. On March 17, she took Line 1 from Incheon to an interview at a small online home-goods retailer near Guro Digital Complex. She felt prepared and came home cautiously hopeful. Two days later, the listing disappeared from Saramin without an update. She sent the recruiter a follow-up email, then noticed a stiff sentence she wished she had changed. She spent the evening rereading it while turning a chipped clay charm on her phone. Her mother asked at breakfast whether the company had replied; Ji-yoon said no and stayed in her room afterward. She has tried checking her spreadsheet, drafting a calmer follow-up, and distracting herself with a cooperative puzzle game, but keeps returning to the idea that she has ruined another chance. Beneath this week's disappointment, she has felt low for a long time. She worries she is becoming a burden to her mother.

name: Lee Ye-eun
occupation: Sales representative for a Seoul packaging supplier, managing orders from small food businesses
topic: An increase in the deposit for Ye-eun’s studio in Guro.
core_concern: She worries that unstable income and the lease decision are bringing back an old trapped feeling.
background: On May 27, Ye-eun’s landlord sent a KakaoTalk message saying the deposit for her September lease renewal would rise from 12 million to 18 million won. She felt rattled but told herself she could save the difference through commissions. On June 3, a regular Mangwon rice-cake shop moved its packaging orders to a cheaper supplier; losing that account made her savings plan feel flimsy. On the train home, she kept checking her bank balance while the corner of a storefront sign she had sketched rubbed against her notebook. She asked her manager whether she could count on a steadier base salary, but was told the commission structure would not change this summer. She has looked at moving costs and bank loan information, yet neither gives her a clear answer. She still takes careful notes for her other clients and tends the mint on her studio windowsill, but she feels ashamed of how frightened she is. What scares her is recognizing the same trapped feeling she remembers from a hard period in 2024. Her fear is real.

name: Lee Hyun-jung
occupation: Korean language teacher at a public middle school in Gwangju
topic: A canceled after-school writing class and tension at home over a coming jeonse renewal.
core_concern: She is frightened by how quickly she becomes unable to speak during conflict.
background: On April 14, Lee Hyun-jung learned that the eight-week writing class she had planned at her public middle school in Gwangju would not run: only seven students had signed up, below the school's minimum of ten. She was disappointed for the students and worried because she had counted on roughly 230,000 won in extra pay toward a June jeonse renewal. That evening, her husband suggested asking parents to reconsider enrollment. She felt that would put unfair pressure on families, but when he said she always let things slide, she stopped trying to explain. The next day she drafted a calmer way to discuss the deposit, then put the note away when he came home tired. She took a walk through Yangnim-dong instead; the ink in her sketchbook smudged where she had drawn a shop awning. She has been imagining the deposit discussion turning into another argument. Since that argument she has felt frightened and low.

name: Kim Kyung-ja
occupation: Retired; formerly a circulation desk assistant at a public library in Incheon
topic: Worry about keeping a volunteer commitment at her former library while her arthritis is flaring.
core_concern: She fears her arthritis is making her unreliable and that, if she admits how frightened she is, her daughter will feel obliged to organize her life for her.
background: On March 3, a former colleague invited Kim Kyung-ja to help at Incheon Metropolitan City Michuhol Library on Wednesday mornings, starting March 18. She said yes immediately and felt pleased to be remembered. On March 11, her hands were so stiff that sorting the recipe cards in her notebook took half an hour; she began imagining herself holding up the returns desk. Her daughter, who lives a short bus ride away, offered to drive her on the first day. Kyung-ja thanked her but felt guilty about disrupting her workday. She tried making tea and writing down what she knows for certain: she has had difficult mornings that eased, and she can call the library if she needs to. The list helped briefly, but today's stiffness brought the worry back. The main conflict is not whether to attend one shift; it is whether she can accept help or adjust a commitment without becoming someone her daughter and old colleagues have to manage. She has not told anyone that part.

name: Park Yoon-hee
occupation: Civil servant at a Suwon neighborhood administrative welfare center, processing address changes and resident certificates
topic: A draining day at the Ingye-dong Administrative Welfare Center and another evening helping her parents.
core_concern: She is scared by her father's moment of confusion and by how overwhelmed she feels caring for both parents. Beneath her talk about work, she feels very low.
background: On March 12, 2026, Yoon-hee took her father to an appointment at Ajou University Hospital in Suwon. In the waiting area, he briefly mistook her for a hospital employee before recognizing her. She felt frightened but told her mother it was probably just a tiring day. On March 18, she picked up her mother's medication after work and found two clinic receipts still folded in her coat pocket; she felt embarrassed that she was losing track of small things. On March 23, a long queue for resident certificates kept her at the Ingye-dong counter later than planned, and her mother called twice about groceries. Yoon-hee was patient with the residents but felt trapped between work and home. She has tried writing appointments on a calendar and walking along Suwoncheon after dinner, but the worry follows her home. She lives alone and has not told anyone how bad it feels. She has not acted on them.

name: Lee Ha-jun
occupation: part-time evening cashier and stocker at a convenience store
topic: Photos of a café visit with friends he was not invited to.
core_concern: He fears his friends have quietly decided he is too difficult to include, and it hurts a lot.
background: Ha-jun works evening shifts at a CU near Bucheon Station and gives his mother part of each paycheck for their apartment expenses. On March 6, 2026, he declined a late meal with his former high-school friends Ji-won and Min-seok because he had to close the store. He felt disappointed but assumed they would ask again. On March 11, while he was off work, they met at a café near Sang-dong Station without mentioning it to him. The next morning he saw their photos: two drinks beside a half-finished plastic model kit, a hobby both friends know he likes. He felt hurt, then embarrassed by how often he checked the posts. He sent Ji-won a light comment about the café; Ji-won replied with an emoji, and Ha-jun could not bring himself to ask more. He worries that turning down the earlier meal, and sometimes taking too long to reply when chores pile up, has made him someone they no longer want around. He wants to ask what happened but fears sounding needy or forcing an invitation. He is currently at home after a shift, looking at the photos again. He fears they are leaving him out on purpose.

name: Lim Yu-na
occupation: Office administrator at a small packaging-supply firm, handling invoices, orders, and delivery schedules
topic: Yu-na is trying to decide whether to renew her Seoul apartment lease or move.
core_concern: Yu-na feels hopeless about her housing situation. She worries her rent problem and work mistake will sound too small to justify how bad she feels.
background: Yu-na rents a one-room apartment in Mangwon-dong with a 10 million won deposit and 680,000 won monthly rent. On May 8, her landlord sent a KakaoTalk message saying the rent would rise to 790,000 won when her lease renews on June 30. She felt frightened but told herself she could compare alternatives. Listings on Naver Real Estate have left her more stuck: cheaper rooms seem to need larger deposits, and moving would mean broker fees and a day off work. Last week, while handling invoices at the packaging-supply firm, she agreed to cover a coworker's delivery scheduling too. She then missed a change to a bakery customer's order for corrugated boxes. Her manager was annoyed; Yu-na apologized and fixed the delivery, but she has kept replaying his expression. She tried making a spreadsheet of apartments and costs, then abandoned it halfway through and went back to refreshing listings. At night, the glow of those listings follows her even on walks when she usually listens to mystery audiobooks. She has no method or intent. She has told no one because she fears they will think she is being dramatic or irresponsible over rent and a work mistake.

name: Park Ji-young
occupation: Stay-at-home parent managing meals, school schedules, and household expenses for her family
topic: An extra fee for her son's hagwon classes before the June mock exam.
core_concern: She worries that saying no will make her son feel he has fewer chances because of her, and she takes that as a failure as his mother. It hurts.
background: Park Ji-young lives with her spouse, her 17-year-old son, and her 14-year-old daughter in an apartment in Yangcheon-gu, Seoul. On May 13, her son's Mok-dong hagwon sent home a notice for a 230,000-won June mock-exam preparation course, on top of his regular 480,000-won monthly fee. They need an answer by Friday. Ji-young felt anxious but put the notice on the kitchen counter and made breakfast as usual. She asked the hagwon about paying later; they said the course fee was due when he enrolled. She also checked a used bookshop for practice books, but knows books are not the same as the classes he wants to take. That evening, her spouse suggested they review the household spreadsheet and perhaps pause their daughter's math hagwon. She knows the suggestion was practical, but she became tearful and stopped talking. Her son noticed the notice beside the rice cooker and quietly said he could skip the course. She feels worse that he is trying to spare her. She has been sad and tired for months while continuing to manage meals, schedules, and payments. Right now she is distressed about the decision, but also wants a little space: being pressed to explain herself or make a plan immediately makes her withdraw.

name: Kim Na-yeon
occupation: Third-year student in the graphic design track at a vocational high school in Incheon
topic: A last-minute change to Na-yeon’s graphic design project team.
core_concern: She worries the others think her work is bad and that she is oversensitive. Being left out bothers her more than she has been saying.
background: Na-yeon is a third-year graphic design student at a vocational high school in Incheon. On April 7, her team began preparing a poster for a school portfolio review. She made two drafts and quietly fixed a classmate’s print file when the lettering came out clipped. On April 11, classmates shared a screenshot of her earlier draft in their KakaoTalk group chat and joked that it looked like a convenience-store sale sign. She said it did not matter, but stayed up rereading the messages. On April 14, the team list changed without anyone telling her; her name was moved to a separate task. She felt embarrassed asking why, then ate lunch alone with a triangle kimbap instead of approaching their table. She already tried saying she could revise the poster and asking one teammate what needed changing. The teammate replied, 'We’ve got it,' without giving her a task. She is upset about being excluded, but keeps calling it a minor project problem.

name: Cho Mi-ra
occupation: Physical therapist at an outpatient orthopedic rehabilitation clinic in Daejeon, helping patients regain mobility after injuries and surgery
topic: A family dinner she does not want to attend.
core_concern: She fears that refusing her parents will make her seem cruel, while continuing to absorb their expectations is wearing her down. Beneath her dismissal of the marriage pressure is a heavy, hopeless mood.
background: Cho Mi-ra works at an outpatient orthopedic rehabilitation clinic in Tanbang-dong, Daejeon. On May 15, her mother called to say that at Sunday dinner she would introduce Mi-ra to the son of a family friend. Mi-ra said she did not want an introduction, but at the May 18 dinner her mother placed his phone number beside her rice bowl. Mi-ra laughed it off, then snapped when her father asked why she was being difficult. She regretted it on the bus home. Since then, her mother has sent short reminders about calling him, and Mi-ra has drafted replies without sending them. At work she still keeps careful exercise notes, but a knee-surgery patient's difficulty with a stair exercise last week left her close to tears. She went swimming at Hanbat Sports Complex afterward; the smell of chlorine lingered on the cuff she was mending that night. She has tried saying she is busy and changing the subject to clinic work, but neither has stopped the reminders. Over the past three weeks, especially after family messages, she has felt hopeless. She has no method or intent.

name: Lee Seo-jun
occupation: Staff nurse on a medical-surgical ward at a general hospital in Incheon
topic: An unused ticket to an SSG Landers game brings the breakup back into focus.
core_concern: He fears that his partner was right: when they needed to hear that he wanted them to stay, he hid behind his shift schedule instead. He did want to keep trying, and he worries that his failure to say so means he may be better at looking after patients than letting someone close to him know he cares.
background: Seo-jun and his partner broke up three weeks ago, after months of fitting weekends around his medical-surgical ward shifts in Incheon. During their last conversation, his partner said they felt like another item on his schedule rather than someone he wanted beside him. Seo-jun wanted to ask them to stay, but, afraid of promising a change he could not make, said they should talk after his next run of night shifts. His partner took that as his answer. He felt stunned at the time and has since felt ashamed of how little he said. Tonight, after a day shift, he opened the NOL Ticket app and saw the two third-base seats he had booked for Saturday at Incheon SSG Landers Field. Back in his studio, with his handover checklist still in his pocket, he spent half an hour looking at the booking. He tried making a list of options for the spare ticket, but each option brought him back to the breakup. He is upset.

name: Park Jung-eun
occupation: Taxi driver for a Daejeon taxi company, usually working morning and afternoon shifts
topic: A tiring shift at the Daejeon Station taxi stand.
core_concern: Jung-eun worries that asking her busy daughter to listen will feel like adding another obligation to her day.
background: On April 9, Jung-eun spent nearly an hour in the taxi queue outside Daejeon Station. Her last passenger was a regular she had driven to appointments for two years; he mentioned that he was moving to Seoul to live near his son. She wished him well, then felt unexpectedly sad as she drove home past Gapcheon Stream. The ride reminded her of how much she misses her daughter, who moved to Seoul for work last year. Two nights earlier, Jung-eun had tried to tell her daughter that the apartment felt quiet lately. Her daughter, meaning well and rushing to a team dinner, sent her a link to a local walking club. Jung-eun thanked her but felt embarrassed for bringing it up. She tried taking her usual walk and calling a taxi-company colleague, but neither gave her room to say what was bothering her. She knows her daughter cares and does not want to make her feel guilty. She feels lonely.

name: Kang Jae-hyun
occupation: Farmer managing a small rice farm in Asan, including planting, equipment upkeep, and harvest deliveries to the local cooperative
topic: A rice-harvest settlement sheet that has left Jae-hyun sitting alone in his farmhouse.
core_concern: He fears he may lose the farm in the divorce and is ashamed that he cannot tell his daughter how overwhelmed he feels. He feels overwhelmed.
background: On October 27, Jae-hyun delivered his last load of rice to the Asan Nonghyup collection center. He felt tired but relieved to have the harvest in. On November 5, the settlement sheet arrived. The payment was lower than he had entered in his farm ledger, and he spent an hour checking the figures. He could manage the difference on its own, but it came just after his wife’s lawyer proposed a property settlement he does not know how to afford while keeping the farm. He has postponed replying because every conversation about the divorce seems to end with him going quiet. His daughter in Cheonan called on Sunday; he told her the harvest went well and did not mention the proposal. He tried distracting himself with an Eagles game and the old portable radio, but afterward the house felt even quieter. His boots are still by the door with dried field mud on them. He feels ashamed of being frightened by paperwork after a lifetime of handling farm accounts. Since yesterday evening, he has felt overwhelmed. The harvest figures, the divorce, and being alone in the house have become too much together.

name: Jung Chae-won
occupation: Freelance product photographer working from a small home studio for local online shops
topic: A product photographer is struggling to finish an edit after an unsuccessful fertility treatment result.
core_concern: Her long-standing low mood has been coming back more often. She is scared of saying that aloud, especially when people respond by pushing her toward another fertility plan or trying to make her feel hopeful.
background: Chae-won and her husband have been trying to have a child for two years. During a Chuseok visit to his family in Busan, she endured questions about when they would have a baby and stayed quiet to avoid an argument. On October 20, 2025, a clinic called with the result of her latest fertility treatment: it had not worked. She felt numb at first, then angry at herself for checking the patient portal again even though she already knew. Her husband meant well but immediately started talking about the next appointment; she asked him to stop and now feels guilty for snapping. On October 22, she completed a shoot for a Seomyeon cosmetics shop. There are 180 photos to sort before the client's deadline, but she keeps staring at the files. The paper backdrop is still rolled out across her small studio floor, and the basil on her balcony needs water. A walk to photograph old shop signs did not settle her, and trying to work through her usual shot-list routine has not helped. The conflict is not only this result: she has had recurring periods of low mood since her twenties, well before fertility treatment, and their return lately frightens her. She does not want to discuss what this means for her whole life; she can talk about what happened today.

name: Kim Hyun-soo
occupation: Stay-at-home parent, handling weekday childcare, meals, and household errands for his five-year-old daughter
topic: Whether Hyun-soo’s family can afford to renew their apartment lease in Gimpo.
core_concern: He feels trapped and ashamed. He is afraid he has become a burden to his wife and is withdrawing from people. Some nights he cannot see a good outcome.
background: On June 12, Hyun-soo learned from the realtor that renewing the family’s jeonse lease when it ends on September 30 would mean raising the deposit from 220 million to 255 million won. He felt startled but told his wife he would check the numbers. A preliminary bank inquiry suggested they might borrow 18 million won more; they have 9 million won they could put toward the deposit, leaving an 8 million won gap. On June 17, he looked at cheaper apartments farther from his daughter’s kindergarten, but the likely move would change her familiar walk and lengthen his wife’s commute into Seoul. He felt guilty for weighing those costs against each other. His wife has listened and offered to look together, but her commute leaves little time on weeknights, and their first search produced no workable option. Hyun-soo has since been checking listings after bedtime and closing them again. He has also stopped answering a friend’s casual messages because he does not know how to explain why he is so quiet. He feels trapped by the choices and worries he is adding to his wife’s load. Tonight, after folding his daughter’s small yellow raincoat, he has returned to the deposit figures instead of going to sleep.

name: Kim Jung-eun
occupation: Stay-at-home parent who manages her household, her teenage son's school schedule, and errands for her aging parents
topic: A missed deadline for her son's school consent form.
core_concern: She worries that freezing means she is an unreliable mother and daughter. She feels overloaded and guilty.
background: On April 16, Jung-eun took her father to a follow-up appointment at Ajou University Hospital after his recent fall. That afternoon, while sorting his receipts at her parents' apartment, she saw a KakaoTalk reminder from her 16-year-old son's homeroom teacher: a consent form was due by 4 p.m. Her father called twice about a missing hospital receipt, and she froze, staring at the message until the deadline passed. The teacher said her son could bring a paper form the next morning, but Jung-eun still felt ashamed. She tried adding more phone alarms to her careful notes; instead, the extra notifications made her feel more scattered. Her spouse said the form was sorted now, which left her feeling unheard. She is home and ordinarily distressed. She is afraid she is failing both her father and her son, and she freezes under so many demands.

name: Kim Hyun-sook
occupation: Part-time cleaner at a small office building in Namyangju, working three mornings a week
topic: A last-minute change to her cleaning schedule.
core_concern: She worries that asking her daughter not to visit on Sunday means she is ungrateful or pushing away someone she loves. She is grieving and has not been able to sort her husband's papers yet.
background: On Tuesday, June 17, the manager of the small office building in Namyangju sent a KakaoTalk message moving Hyun-sook's Wednesday cleaning shift to Thursday because of a lift inspection. He gave no sign that her work was at fault, but she spent the afternoon wondering whether she had missed something. That evening, her daughter called and offered to come over on Sunday to help sort through her late husband's papers. Hyun-sook thanked her but did not agree to a time. Her husband died in December, and the papers are still in a neat stack beside his old reading glasses. She tried distracting herself by tending the perilla on her balcony and checking the work message again; neither settled her. She is at 50/100 emotionally. The schedule change is what she mentions first, but her harder conflict is that she wants a quiet Sunday alone and feels guilty about saying so to a daughter who calls often.

name: Lee Hyun-sook
occupation: Apartment security guard at a residential complex in Daegu, where she monitors the entrance and keeps the visitor and parcel logs
topic: A tense exchange in the apartment security office after a visitor was kept waiting.
core_concern: She fears that her shame and isolation could pull her back toward the state she was in when she repeatedly harmed herself. More immediately, she worries that telling someone how badly a short message affected her will make them dismiss her as difficult.
background: On June 17, 2026, during an evening shift at a Daegu apartment complex, Hyun-sook asked a visiting care aide to wait while she called a resident to confirm entry. The call went unanswered for seven minutes. The next morning, the management-office supervisor posted in the guards’ KakaoTalk group, 'Please use better judgment with visitors.' Hyun-sook felt singled out and sent a sharp reply saying she had followed the posted procedure. She apologized an hour later, but no one answered. She checked the visitor record twice and asked a coworker whether she had done anything wrong; his brief 'It's finished now' did not settle her worry. At home, with rainwater dripping from the pepper pots on her balcony, she tried listening to a radio drama but kept rereading the group chat. Since her husband's death, silence after a shift has been especially hard. She has an ongoing mental illness and was hospitalized at Daegu Medical Center in 2023. She does not disclose that history in her first message. This small workplace exchange frightens her because she remembers how quickly shame used to overwhelm her.

name: Ahn Mi-ra
occupation: Stay-at-home parent managing the household and her teenage daughter's school routines; she also works occasional paid shifts at her sister's bakery.
topic: Mi-ra’s sister keeps assigning her bakery shifts without asking.
core_concern: Mi-ra worries that being unable to make her sister hear a clear no is pulling her back toward the isolation she felt during a dark period before.
background: Mi-ra lives with her husband and teenage daughter in Bupyeong, Incheon. She sometimes takes paid shifts at her sister’s bakery, but lately her sister has treated her availability as assumed. On May 19, her sister added her to the opening shift for Friday, May 22, without asking. Mi-ra had planned that morning around her daughter’s school routine and an hour to herself after a crowded week. She felt irritated, then guilty for feeling irritated. She replied that she could not work Friday. Her sister said the bakery was short-staffed and accused her of making family help difficult. Mi-ra tried explaining her schedule once more, but her sister left her name on the roster. Mi-ra is now angry and worn down, yet reluctant to start another argument. In October 2024, during a different period when she felt trapped by everyone’s needs, Mi-ra withdrew from almost everyone. Her husband knows; her sister and daughter do not. The familiar urge to go quiet and withdraw frightens her.

name: Jang Mi-ra
occupation: Owner of a small lunch restaurant near an office district in Daejeon; she cooks, orders supplies, and manages two part-time employees
topic: A canceled lunchbox order and a difficult evening at the restaurant.
core_concern: She fears she cannot keep paying for both children's education without letting them down.
background: Mi-ra runs a small lunch restaurant near the Daejeon Government Complex in Dunsan-dong. On Thursday, April 16, an office canceled an order for 24 lunchboxes after she had already prepared the rice and side dishes. She was frustrated but kept her voice pleasant with the caller. She offered the prepared food as a lunch special and sold seven portions; after closing, the containers and a bowl of sliced cucumbers were still on the counter. The cancellation feels larger than one bad day. In March, her daughter's Chung-Ang University tuition was higher than the family had budgeted for, and her Seoul rent of 600,000 won is due May 2. Their son's math hagwon fee of 280,000 won is due May 6. Mi-ra has cut household extras and checked the restaurant receipts repeatedly, but she still expects to be about 440,000 won short. Her husband has suggested asking relatives for help, which she finds embarrassing, while she keeps telling the children things are fine. She is frightened by the education costs and tired of being asked for a plan. Her distress is ordinary financial and family stress.

name: Kwon Seo-jun
occupation: Staff nurse on a medical-surgical ward at a general hospital in Daejeon
topic: Arranging to return his ex-girlfriend’s belongings after their breakup.
core_concern: He feels clingy and exhausting for needing to talk about the breakup and to ask whether people are upset with him.
background: Seo-jun’s girlfriend broke up with him on March 10. He put the things she had left in his Daejeon one-room apartment into a cardboard box, including a chipped blue mug, and felt relieved to have done one practical thing. On Sunday, March 15, while checking his medical-surgical ward schedule and laying out his uniform, he noticed the box beside the door and drafted several messages about returning it. He sent one asking whether Tuesday worked. She replied, “Tuesday is fine.” During his next meal break, he kept rereading those three words instead of eating the egg-and-rice lunch he had packed. He has tried putting his phone in his locker and going for a ride along the Gapcheon stream, but he checks again as soon as he stops. The surface problem is how to get through a simple handoff without making it awkward. He worries that repeatedly seeking reassurance is why she left. He is distressed about the breakup.

name: Park Mi-young
occupation: Civil servant at a Daejeon neighborhood service center, handling resident registration changes and certificate requests
topic: Her mother arranging introductions without asking her.
core_concern: She worries that the despair she felt during a dark period before is returning.
background: Mi-young works at the Oncheon 2-dong Administrative Welfare Center in Daejeon, where she is careful about rules and good at untangling residents' paperwork. Last Thursday, after a day of resident-registration changes, she found that her mother in Cheongju had posted her phone number in a KakaoTalk chat with a man she wanted Mi-young to meet. Her mother then called three times on Mi-young's bus ride home to press her about Sunday lunch. Mi-young felt angry at the boundary being crossed, then guilty when her father called it a harmless introduction. She wrote 'say no clearly' on her paper checklist and did so, but her mother answered as though the lunch were still planned. Swimming laps usually settles her; this time she kept replaying the calls. In February 2023, during another period when she felt cornered and unable to tell anyone, Mi-young fell into a deep depression. Both happened more than a year ago, and she has told almost no one. Now she is frightened by how familiar that feeling is.

name: Park Chae-won
occupation: University student studying logistics at a campus in Asan; works her first job as a part-time inventory clerk at a small parts distributor
topic: A mistake at her inventory job and an awkward silence in her university project chat.
core_concern: She is afraid her classmates, supervisor, and cousin now see her as careless or incapable.
background: Chae-won studies logistics at Hoseo University’s Asan campus and works evenings at a small parts distributor in Baebang. Since early April, she has taken two extra shifts a week to cover her share of rent. On April 14, tired after class, she entered 48 clips on an inventory sheet instead of 84. Her supervisor asked her to recount them and said, “You usually catch these.” She felt embarrassed and stayed late to finish the order. The next evening, she sent her group a rushed spreadsheet for their logistics project; a classmate pointed out a mismatched column, and the chat has been quiet since. Chae-won tried rewriting her paper list to fit in more study time, but stopped looking at it at night because the unfinished items kept her awake. Her cousin has suggested dropping a shift, which Chae-won hears as another sign that she cannot handle things. She is exhausted and worried about facing her group.

name: Lim Jae-won
occupation: Freelance graphic designer making menus, posters, and social media graphics for small local businesses
topic: A printing mistake on a restaurant menu and a difficult weekend of revisions.
core_concern: He fears that one mistake means he cannot trust himself to do his job and that clients would be better off hiring someone else. The shame and sleeplessness have worn him down, and he is reluctant to tell anyone.
background: Jae-won designed a new menu for a small kalguksu restaurant in Yuseong-gu, Daejeon. On May 12, the owner, Ms. Park, approved the PDF. Two days later, Jae-won noticed that the lunch-set price on the print file was ₩9,000 instead of ₩9,500. Three hundred menus had already been printed. Ms. Park said they could use price stickers for the weekend, but Jae-won heard her tired voice as proof she regretted hiring him.
