He paid for a corrected print run himself and spent Friday night checking the matching Instagram graphics, zooming in until the letters blurred. He tried taking a walk to photograph old shop signs near his apartment and starting a co-op game with a friend, but kept returning to the files. By Sunday, he was exhausted and ashamed, despite having fixed the error.

name: Choi Jun-ho
occupation: Middle-school math instructor at a neighborhood hagwon in Daejeon
topic: A mistake in a math handout and the parent complaint that followed.
core_concern: He worries that his careful, dependable self is slipping under the strain of teaching and caring for his parents. Beneath the complaint, he feels hopeless and frightened by how familiar it feels after a dark period in 2022.
background: Jun-ho teaches middle-school math at a neighborhood hagwon in Daejeon. On April 17, he handed out a practice sheet for an upcoming school exam with an incorrect answer key. A parent posted a photo of it in the class KakaoTalk chat, and the hagwon director asked him to send a correction before his 4 p.m. class. He did, but felt exposed and kept checking the chat for more complaints. That morning he had taken his father to a follow-up appointment at Chungnam National University Hospital; the corrected sheet was still on his desk beside an untouched convenience-store kimbap when he got home. He has tried rechecking every handout and telling the director he is fine, but the mistake keeps replaying in his head. Since late March, difficult evenings have left him feeling hopeless.

name: Yoon Jae-won
occupation: Second-year student at a middle school in Busan
topic: A disappointing math-hagwon test and another class added to Jae-won's schedule.
core_concern: He worries that school pressure getting to him this much makes him weak or dramatic.
background: On Friday, March 13, Jae-won scored 71 out of 100 on a diagnostic test at his math hagwon in Busan's Yeonsan-dong. He had expected to do better and felt embarrassed when he folded the score sheet into his backpack beside a half-finished futsal video edit. The next evening, his parents added a Thursday class that runs until 9:30 p.m. His mother called it a head start for university; Jae-won heard it as proof that his effort did not count. He tried saying the extra class would leave no time for futsal or editing, but the conversation became an argument about his future. Since then he has been quieter at home. He still wants his parents to notice something is wrong, but worries they will think he is making excuses.

name: Lee Da-eun
occupation: Full-time candidate for the Jeju provincial general administrative civil service exam; studies at a Jeju City library and at home
topic: Da-eun cannot bring herself to review a disappointing civil-service mock exam.
core_concern: She fears she is becoming a burden to her mother and that failing the exam would make all her mother's patience and support feel wasted. She has been avoiding her mother too, because even an ordinary question about studying makes her feel like a disappointment.
background: On May 9, Da-eun took a timed mock exam at a hagwon in Nohyeong-dong. She scored 62, down from 79 the month before, with the Jeju provincial exam approaching in June. She felt stunned on the bus home, then ashamed when her mother asked how it went while putting away groceries. Da-eun said only that it was difficult. The next day at the Jeju City library, she opened her answer sheet but spent an hour rearranging her study plan instead of checking her mistakes. She tried making a shorter review list at home, but left that unfinished too. Now two days have passed, and the folded answer sheet is still in her bag beside a library receipt. She has stopped replying to a study-group chat. She worries that her mother is carrying the household errands and expenses while she produces nothing to show for it. The score and the lost days hurt.

name: Shin Ji-min
occupation: Administrative assistant at a small packaging-design firm in Seoul, handling invoices, schedules, and client emails
topic: A corrected delivery mistake at work that Ji-min cannot stop replaying.
core_concern: Ji-min fears that needing reassurance after an already-fixed mistake makes her burdensome. She feels embarrassed and hurt at being dismissed.
background: This morning at a small packaging-design firm in Mapo, Ji-min arranged a courier for sample boxes going to a client's Seongsu showroom. She copied the old entrance from a previous request, noticed the mismatch when the courier called at 11:18, and corrected it. The boxes arrived before the client's 2 p.m. review, and her manager confirmed that nothing had been delayed. Ji-min felt briefly relieved, then embarrassed when a coworker brushed off her attempt to explain why she had been rattled. On the Line 2 ride home, she replayed both the mistake and her coworker's reaction. She has checked the delivery confirmation twice and drafted, but not sent, an apologetic KakaoTalk message to her manager. Now she is in her Mangwon studio with a triangle kimbap still unopened on the table. The delivery is resolved; what has not settled is the feeling that her worry is an inconvenience to other people.

name: Shin Ki-hyun
occupation: Stay-at-home parent managing the household and school-day routines for his two children
topic: An argument about school expenses and the work of managing the household.
core_concern: He feels hurt, not just worried about the spending. The argument has brought back the shame and hopelessness he remembers from a dark period in 2023. He worries that admitting this will make his spouse see him as incapable of caring for the children.
background: On March 18, 2026, Ki-hyun paid a 48,000-won school activity fee through the e알리미 notice for his nine-year-old and renewed his twelve-year-old’s 260,000-won math hagwon enrollment. That evening, his spouse noticed both charges and asked why they had not discussed them first. Ki-hyun understood the concern about money, but felt that keeping track of notices, deadlines, and pickups had become invisible until a payment appeared. He defended the expenses, then apologized for his tone. He lay awake replaying the exchange while a damp taekwondo uniform hung over the bathroom door. They had already tried a shared expense spreadsheet and a Sunday check-in, but both fell away when the week got busy. He now has the numbers ready and wants a practical way to raise them, though another budget discussion feels inadequate. His spouse knows it happened, but they have rarely spoken about it since. What unsettles him is how familiar his sense of failure feels.

name: Hong Na-yeon
occupation: Civil service exam candidate preparing for a grade 9 general administration post in Gyeonggi Province; studies most weekdays at a public library in Paju
topic: A disappointing civil service practice exam and a difficult week at the library.
core_concern: She worries that failing the exam will confirm she has wasted her savings and her parents' patience. The pressure frightens her.
background: On March 10, Na-yeon took a Gongdangi practice exam for the Gyeonggi Province grade 9 general administration post. Her average was 62, down from 71 the previous month; administrative law was 45. She felt ashamed, especially because she recognized mistakes she had made before. For the next two days at Paju Central Library, she spent hours color-coding those mistakes instead of retrying the questions. At dinner on March 12, her father asked whether she had considered returning to office work. He meant it as a practical question, but she heard it as proof that he had lost confidence in her. She said she was fine, then took an evening walk and photographed the peeling blue sign outside a closed stationery shop. She has tried making a stricter timetable and brushing off her parents' questions, but neither has eased the pressure. Now she is at her usual end-of-row library seat, unable to start a practice set. She has not told anyone how much the pressure frightens her. She feels frightened and ashamed.

name: Lee Su-bin
occupation: Job seeker applying for junior operations coordinator roles at e-commerce companies in Seoul
topic: A rejection after an operations coordinator interview in Seoul.
core_concern: She worries that one spreadsheet mistake proves she is not capable of doing the jobs she applies for. She is especially ashamed that she cannot bring herself to update her carefully kept application tracker.
background: On March 17, Su-bin traveled from Bucheon to Guro Digital Complex for an interview at a small e-commerce company. During a short spreadsheet exercise, she noticed too late that she had sorted a returns column incorrectly. She left feeling cautiously hopeful because the interviewer had asked when she could start. On March 19, a brief rejection email arrived while she was on Line 1. She read it beside a window fogged by someone’s takeaway coffee, then closed her application spreadsheet without recording the result. Her roommate thinks she is still waiting to hear back. Su-bin has tried replaying the exercise to work out whether that mistake cost her the job, but it has only made her avoid the spreadsheet. She has not explained the whole search to her roommate. She is distressed and ashamed.

name: Choi Eun-sook
occupation: Senior public job program worker who tidies reading tables and restocks notices at a neighborhood library in Daegu three mornings a week
topic: A mistake with notices during her morning shift at the library.
core_concern: She worries that her age and carefulness are no longer enough, and that coworkers may see her as a burden and eventually stop giving her work. She feels embarrassed and worried, given what the job means to her.
background: On her Tuesday morning shift at Daegu Metropolitan Suseong Library, Eun-sook restocked the reading-room notice stand with flyers for a spring reading event. Near noon, a coworker noticed that she had used an older stack with the wrong registration date. Eun-sook replaced them before leaving; the coworker said it was an easy mistake, and the supervisor simply reminded her to check dates. Still, she felt embarrassed all the way home on the bus. On Thursday she checked every notice twice, then apologized to the coworker again, who seemed puzzled by the apology. She has tried telling herself that no one was harmed, but she keeps picturing someone deciding she is too slow for the three-mornings-a-week job. Her program wages help cover rent and utilities, and the library is one of the few places where she feels useful. This small mistake has stayed with her.

name: Lim Chae-won
occupation: Civil service exam candidate preparing for the local government administrative service exam at a study café
topic: A disappointing civil service mock-exam score and an awkward dinner with her mother.
core_concern: She feels the exam score is not the only problem. She is frightened by how much an old crisis has been on her mind.
background: Chae-won is preparing for the Gyeonggi-do local government administrative service exam at a study café in Suwon. On March 14, 2026, her mock-exam average fell from 78 to 68, with Korean history dropping to 55. She copied the missed questions into her notebook, but by Monday she was still rereading the score instead of reviewing them. At dinner, her mother asked whether she should consider office work again if the exam does not go well. Chae-won knows her mother worries about their grocery costs, yet heard the question as a loss of faith in her. She tried making a new study timetable and calling her friend Min-ji on the walk home; neither quieted the worry. She even photographed a neighborhood cat sitting beside a crushed milk carton, then felt guilty for stopping. She is now at the study café, struggling to concentrate.

name: Jang Na-yeon
occupation: Second-year student at a public middle school in Daejeon
topic: Being left out of lunch plans and dreading the school cafeteria.
core_concern: She worries that snapping at Minji makes her look needy or mean.
background: Na-yeon is a second-year student at a public middle school in Daejeon. On March 12, she saw three friends arranging where to sit at lunch in their group chat without asking her. She felt embarrassed but told herself it might happen only once. On March 16, they did it again. She asked Minji whether there was room at their table; Minji replied, “idk,” and Na-yeon spent the evening rereading it instead of practicing a pop song on her borrowed keyboard. On March 18, Na-yeon stood in the cafeteria holding her tray while the friends waved another classmate into the last open seat. The metal chopsticks kept sliding against the tray as she looked for somewhere else to sit. Later, she snapped at Minji in the hallway, asking why sitting with her had become a problem. Minji said she was making it a big deal and walked away. Na-yeon has already tried asking directly and acting as though nothing happened; neither made lunch feel easier. She is now dreading tomorrow’s lunch and feels both hurt by the exclusion and ashamed of how sharply she spoke.

name: Kim Eun-young
occupation: Owner and sole tailor at a clothing alterations shop in Ssangyong-dong, Cheonan
topic: A canceled school-uniform alterations order and a difficult evening at the shop.
core_concern: She fears the hopelessness she remembers from a dark period before is returning. She fears being seen as a bad mother.
background: On Monday, a parent from her daughter’s school brought in six uniforms for alterations. Eun-young stayed late marking the hems with blue tailor’s chalk, relieved that the work would cover a good part of this month’s shop rent. The next afternoon, the parent canceled the order before she had sewn anything. Eun-young said she understood, but kept checking the empty space in her order book. At home, her daughter noticed her mood and offered to help sort receipts; Eun-young snapped at her, then apologized. She has tried taking a walk through Cheonan Samgeori Park and watching a Hanwha Eagles game on her phone, but neither has quieted her fear that she is becoming someone her daughter has to tiptoe around. Tonight she is frightened by how familiar her hopelessness feels, though she has not said that aloud.

topic: Four rejected crates of lettuce and whether he can keep up with the greenhouses.
core_concern: He fears his worsening health is turning him into a burden on his wife and that he cannot be counted on to keep their livelihood going. Underneath that fear is a hopeless mood he is ashamed to admit.
background: Kang Jae-hyun leases two greenhouses outside Gwangju and delivers leafy greens to a stallholder at Yangdong Market. On May 14, a ventilation motor stopped during a warm spell. He noticed browned leaf edges early, but between his knee pain and the morning deliveries, he could not sort every tray as carefully as usual. On May 27, the stallholder returned four of 22 crates of lettuce. Jae-hyun was embarrassed and immediately pictured losing the account, though the stallholder had not said that. His wife helped carry the crates back to their truck, then took on more sorting the next day. He offered to do the next delivery alone, but his knee hurt too much to load the truck; he tried making a fresh order list, then left it unfinished on the kitchen table. Their greenhouse lease comes up for discussion in June, and he fears asking his wife to shoulder another season. He has no method or intent. He was hospitalized for depression nine years ago and fears that admitting these thoughts will alarm his wife. A few returned crates feel much larger to him than they look.

name: Kwon Ji-min
occupation: Stay-at-home parent and primary caregiver for her three-year-old daughter
topic: A family lunch that turned into another argument about marriage.
core_concern: Ji-min feels no one takes her hurt seriously until she gets sharp, and that her anger means she is failing the people she loves. Being cornered at her daughter's celebration hurt, and how overwhelmed she feels frightens her.
background: On May 16, 2026, Ji-min took her three-year-old daughter and longtime partner to a birthday lunch with her mother near Mangwon Market. Her mother asked, in front of everyone, when they would finally register their marriage at the Mapo-gu office. Ji-min felt exposed and angry; her partner changed the subject instead of backing her up. When her daughter grew tired and began picking the sesame seeds off a dumpling, Ji-min took her home early. She has asked her mother before to stop raising marriage at family meals and has asked her partner to speak up, but neither conversation changed much. At home, her partner said her mother meant well. Ji-min snapped at him and now feels ashamed of that, too. She has kept her daughter's routine going, but she is replaying the lunch whenever the apartment gets quiet.

name: Jang Dong-hyun
occupation: Job seeker applying for entry-level office assistant and inventory clerk roles in Daejeon
topic: Dong-hyun keeps reorganizing his job-application spreadsheet instead of submitting an application.
core_concern: Dong-hyun fears that his inability to submit an application he cares about means he will never become independent and is becoming a burden to his parents. He feels trapped between wanting the job and fearing another rejection.
background: In February 2026, Dong-hyun applied through Work24 for an inventory clerk role near Daejeon Industrial Complex. He checked every requirement, rewrote his cover letter for two evenings, and felt cautiously hopeful when he submitted it. The rejection on February 19 left him embarrassed, though he told his parents that competition was probably high. He then attended a résumé session at the Daejeon Employment Welfare Plus Center. He made the suggested edits but still found himself rewriting individual sentences for hours. Now an office assistant posting in Seo-gu closes on March 6. He has the documents ready, yet keeps adjusting his spreadsheet instead of applying. His mother has noticed him staying at the kitchen table after midnight, beside a cold mug of barley tea; he says he is nearly done. He has also declined his school friend's last two co-op game invitations and stopped taking his usual evening walks along the Gapcheon. He worries that, while his parents make room for him at home, he is making no progress toward supporting himself. He feels stuck and hopeless.

name: Lee Su-ah
occupation: Job seeker applying for entry-level inventory and office support roles at Daegu logistics companies
topic: A confusing pay offer and rejection from a Daegu logistics job.
core_concern: The rejection has stirred up thoughts about not wanting to exist, and she is afraid that saying so will make someone panic, dismiss her, or take control of the conversation.
background: On March 6, Su-ah saved a Saramin listing for an entry-level inventory and office support role at a company in Daegu’s Seongseo Industrial Complex. It showed 2.35 million won a month, but the recruiter’s March 10 text described 2.15 million won in base pay plus a variable attendance allowance. She noticed the difference immediately. She had submitted her application just before the deadline, after losing track of which résumé file was final among her phone notes and browser tabs, and spent the next day worrying she had attached the wrong one. On March 12, she got a rejection text; that evening she saw the role reposted with the pay phrased differently again. She felt angry at the company, then embarrassed that she still wanted them to call. Her older sister, with whom she shares rent, asked about the search while they were eating convenience-store pudding. Su-ah snapped, then apologized. She has tried putting applications in a spreadsheet, but stopped updating it after a few days; her sister’s offer to check her résumé felt like another inspection. For the past month, setbacks have left her feeling hopeless. She has not told her sister about the current thoughts. Right now she is rereading the reposted listing.

name: Lee Ji-woo
occupation: Recently laid off from an order-coordinator role at a small furniture distributor in Gimpo
topic: An unsettling visit to the Gimpo Employment Welfare Plus Center after being laid off.
core_concern: She feels ashamed of being unemployed and of struggling with it.
background: Ji-woo was laid off from a small furniture distributor in Gimpo at the end of March. On April 18, she went to the Gimpo Employment Welfare Plus Center for her first unemployment-benefit appointment. She had prepared every document in a clear folder, but while waiting with a numbered ticket, she ran into a former coworker, Min-seo. Their conversation was friendly and brief; afterward, Ji-woo kept replaying her own awkward answers. At home, she rearranged the green onions on her balcony and checked Employment24, where a recent application still showed only that it had been viewed. Neither task settled her. She has tried making lists and keeping busy, but the encounter keeps returning to her mind. The main conflict is that she wants to be honest with people close to her, yet fears they will see her unemployment as evidence that she failed.

name: Lee Hyun-jung
occupation: Office administrator handling invoices and supplier orders at a small stationery wholesaler in Seoul
topic: An incorrect supplier order and a meeting with her manager tomorrow.
core_concern: She fears her manager will decide she is incapable and that she cannot keep meeting both her work and family responsibilities.
background: On 14 October, Hyun-jung entered an order for 630 A4 ring binders instead of 360 at the small stationery wholesaler in Euljiro where she handles supplier orders. She usually catches errors like this, but she was rushing to leave for her seven-year-old daughter's after-school pickup. The extra cartons arrived on 16 October. Her manager noticed during stock intake and asked her to explain the order at 9 a.m. tomorrow. She felt embarrassed, then frightened that the one thing she is good at—being careful—no longer counts. A colleague told her it would probably be fine; she answered bluntly and spent the subway ride home worrying about that, too. She has checked the order record and drafted an explanation twice, but each attempt has made her more afraid of sounding incapable. Tonight her daughter is asleep and her husband is still at work.

name: Park Myung-hee
occupation: Head of general affairs at a mid-sized publishing company in Seoul
topic: A clash between preparations for the Seoul International Book Fair and her father’s hospital appointment.
core_concern: She fears that taking responsibility for everyone until she is exhausted could bring her back to how she felt in late 2022. She does not know how to share the load without feeling like a burden or a bad daughter.
background: On Monday, 16 June 2025, Myung-hee promised to oversee shipping labels and staff supplies for her publishing company’s stand at the Seoul International Book Fair. She also said she would take her father to an appointment at Seoul Asan Medical Center on Wednesday, 18 June, although her younger brother had offered to go. On Wednesday morning, a colleague needed her to resolve a delivery mix-up while her father was waiting to leave. Myung-hee asked her brother to take him after all, then worried that her request sounded like criticism for not having stepped in sooner. At work, she apologized for arriving late, even though the team had managed without her. She tried making a more detailed list for the following week, but it only showed her how much she had agreed to do. The resemblance between her exhaustion now and how she felt then frightens her. She is afraid that asking her brother to take an errand will seem selfish.

name: Lee Geon-woo
occupation: Full-time candidate for Seoul’s grade-9 general administration civil service exam, studying through online lectures and at a public library
topic: A disappointing civil service mock-exam score and a study day that slipped away.
core_concern: He feels pressure to show his parents that their support is paying off, and even friendly check-ins have begun to feel like requests for a progress report. He fears that avoiding Min-jae's calls makes him ungrateful and a bad friend.
background: Geon-woo is preparing for Seoul’s grade-9 general administration exam using Gongdangi lectures and a desk at Eunpyeong Public Library. On May 9, he scored 68 on a full mock exam, down from 74 two weeks earlier; administrative law was his weakest subject. He felt shaken but told himself the score was useful information. On May 12, he rewrote his study spreadsheet, added extra administrative-law lectures, and skipped his Sunday ride along Bulgwangcheon. By May 15, he had spent so much time adjusting the plan that he had barely begun the questions he meant to review. At dinner, his mother gently asked how the new schedule was working. He said 'fine' and felt guilty afterward: his parents pay his living costs, and he knows she meant well. He has also stopped calling his friend Min-jae on the walk home because another conversation about preparation feels exhausting. The revised schedule, longer lectures, and canceled ride have not helped him settle back into studying. He is at home now, looking at his study log and an unopened lunch container in his bag. He worries that saying so would sound ungrateful.

name: Kim Hyun-jung
occupation: Real-estate agent at a small neighborhood brokerage in Pyeongtaek, handling apartment rentals and sales
topic: A slow month at her Pyeongtaek brokerage and an upcoming mortgage payment.
core_concern: She feels ashamed of struggling with her mortgage.
background: Kim Hyun-jung lives alone in a mortgaged apartment in Pyeongtaek. On February 14, 2026, an apartment rental she had spent weeks arranging fell through when the landlord could not return the previous tenant's deposit on time. She had counted on the commission to help cover her March 25 mortgage payment of 1.18 million won. At first she felt disappointed but kept booking viewings; by early March, with no replacement deal, she felt ashamed each time she checked her account. She has cut small expenses and made a list of what she can pay, but the list does not close the gap. She keeps postponing a call to the bank because she dreads explaining her situation. The brokerage owner knows business is slow but not how tight things are for her; her younger sister sends cheerful KakaoTalk messages that Kim answers without mentioning money. She has no method or intent. She worries that admitting either her financial trouble or those thoughts will make someone see her as irresponsible.

name: Park Soo-yeon
occupation: Owner and sole operator of a clothing alterations shop near Pyeongtaek Station
topic: A tiring week of school-uniform alterations and household expenses.
core_concern: She fears she is failing her children when the shop cannot reliably cover their education costs.
background: In the first week of March 2026, Soo-yeon's shop near Pyeongtaek Station filled with last-minute school-uniform alterations. On March 4, she stayed after closing to finish a student's trousers; a little blue tailor's chalk was still on her sleeve when she got home. She felt useful but exhausted. That evening, she saw that her daughter's middle-school math hagwon fee of 310,000 won was due on March 10, alongside 78,000 won for her younger son's elementary-school after-school class. February had been a slow month at the shop. She checked the accounts twice, set aside the week's cash receipts, and found that the numbers still felt tight. When she mentioned it to her husband, he suggested pausing the hagwon for a month. She knows he meant to help, but their daughter has been anxious about keeping up with her new class, and the suggestion left Soo-yeon feeling more alone with the decision. She has tried working longer hours and quietly cutting small purchases, neither of which has eased her worry. For now, she speaks about the busy shop and how tired she feels. It is heavy to keep making these decisions.

name: Shin Da-eun
occupation: First-year student in the culinary arts track at a vocational high school in Chungju
topic: An argument at home after a culinary-school practical assessment.
core_concern: Da-eun fears that her parents see one disappointing score as proof that her effort and her choice of school do not count.
background: On May 16, Da-eun scored 72 out of 100 on a baking practical because her madeleines browned unevenly. She was embarrassed, especially after staying late twice that week to practice; she can still picture the condensation clouding the lid of the container she carried home. On May 19, her mother saw the score and asked whether Da-eun had been staying after school because she was struggling. Da-eun showed her practice notebook, hoping it would show how hard she was working. Instead, her parents talked about whether she should leave the culinary track next semester. Da-eun sent an angry message from the bus near Chungju Jungang Market, then apologized for its wording. The apology seemed to make her parents think she agreed with them. She is now at home, dreading another conversation about school. Their doubt hurts.

name: Lee Seo-yun
occupation: Civil service exam candidate preparing for a municipal administrative clerk position
topic: A disappointing mock-exam score during preparation for the municipal clerk exam.
core_concern: She fears that admitting how badly the score affected her will make her seem weak or lazy.
background: Seo-yun is preparing for the June 20 local-government grade-9 exam. At a Suwon hagwon mock exam on May 9, she scored 78, below the 85 she had set as her target. She lost several points on local-autonomy questions she thought she knew. On the bus home, she kept reopening the answer sheet while a bag of madeleines she had baked for her study friend sat untouched on her lap. Her friend thanked her for the notes she had shared earlier that week, which felt good for a moment, then made Seo-yun wonder why she can be patient with someone else's mistakes but not her own. That evening, her mother casually asked how the mock exam went. Seo-yun said it was fine, then spent three hours rechecking answers instead of taking her usual walk to photograph neighborhood cats. She tried making a revised study timetable the next morning, but every block looked like evidence that she was behind. She is tired and upset. She has not told anyone how ashamed she feels.

name: Choi Su-bin
occupation: First-year student at a middle school in Daegu
topic: Being left out of a school science project and mocked in the class chat.
core_concern: She worries that something is wrong with her.
background: On November 9, 2026, Su-bin's class 1-3 science group began a poster about the Geumho River. Three classmates divided the work in their KakaoTalk chat without including her. She felt angry but decided to draw a neat map in her graph-paper notebook so she could still contribute. On November 12, they submitted the poster with her name on it but did not use her drawing. That evening, one classmate joked in the chat that Su-bin was 'good at doing nothing,' and the others reacted with laughing emojis. She showed the messages to her homeroom teacher, Ms. Kim, who told the group to include everyone next time. Su-bin felt briefly relieved, then embarrassed when a classmate called her a tattletale. She now takes a longer route home through Beomeo-dong to avoid seeing them after school; her mother only knows she has been getting home late. She fears that telling an adult more will make things worse.

name: Song Su-bin
occupation: Kindergarten teacher leading a class of five-year-olds at a private kindergarten in Seoul
topic: A parent’s message about a kindergarten field-trip photo.
core_concern: She fears the parent’s brief reply means she failed a child, but she also needs time alone instead of more questions or reassurance. She worries that needing space makes her seem uncaring.
background: On Thursday, March 19, Su-bin took her class of 19 five-year-olds to the Seoul Children’s Museum in Gwangjin-gu. She had made buddy cards so no child would be left out. During a group photo, one child was inside with the assistant teacher washing their hands. That evening, the child’s parent saw the photo on Kids Note and asked why their child was missing. Su-bin checked the other photos, confirmed the child had joined the activities, and sent a careful explanation. The parent replied only, ‘알겠습니다.’ Su-bin felt relieved for a moment, then began worrying that the short reply meant the parent was upset. She asked a senior teacher to read her response; the teacher said it was clear, but that did not settle her. On Friday she stayed late preparing Monday’s activity and kept reopening the message while her pocket sketchbook lay untouched in her bag. She is home in her small studio now, tired but not in danger. She wants some quiet. When people press her to talk or fix things, she withdraws and then feels guilty for doing so.

name: Jang Mi-young
occupation: Home-care worker with a Cheonan agency, visiting older clients to help with meals, washing, and daily routines
topic: An agency message about a home-care visit log is weighing on Mi-young.
core_concern: She has been doing unpaid extra work and is frightened that setting a boundary will make her seem uncaring or cost her shifts. She also worries that telling a friend or her husband how much this hurts will make her a burden.
background: Mi-young works for a home-care agency in Cheonan. For several months, she has been staying a little past her scheduled visits with an older client in Ssangyong-dong because the client's son often asks her to do one more task before she leaves. She has not recorded the extra time or told her supervisor; saying no feels unkind, but staying late has left her tired and behind on her other visits. On May 12, she finished the agreed tasks and left at the scheduled time, despite another request. The son then complained to the agency that his mother had been left without proper help. On May 14, the agency texted Mi-young to discuss her visit log the next morning. She has reread the message repeatedly and feels both hurt by the complaint and uneasy about explaining the unrecorded time. She once tried telling the son what time her visit ended, but backed down when he said his mother depended on her. At home, she has drafted and erased a message to her supervisor. Her husband is working late, and she is considering calling a friend but worries she has already complained too much lately.

name: Jeon Tae-yang
occupation: First-year student at a public high school in Seoul
topic: He cannot stop checking his midterm rank and has started skipping badminton.
core_concern: He worries that his disappointing rank and his parents' spending on hagwon mean he is becoming a burden. His withdrawal frightens him: he feels stuck, increasingly hopeless about catching up, and unsure how to tell someone close to him without disappointing them.
background: On May 13, Tae-yang saw that he ranked 87th out of 226 first-year students after his first midterms at a public high school in Yangcheon-gu. He had expected to do better and felt embarrassed when a friend casually mentioned ranking 19th. That evening, his mother reminded him about his Tuesday and Thursday math hagwon in Mok-dong. He knows she meant to help, but he thought about what his parents spend on it and felt like a burden. Over the next few days, he repeatedly opened the school grade page, rearranged his EBSi study notes instead of using them, and lay awake worrying about the time he had lost. On Friday, he skipped pickup badminton at the Yangcheon-gu Sports Center and left his friend's KakaoTalk message unanswered. Even his younger brother noticed he had stopped sketching subway maps with him. On a walk home, Tae-yang photographed a handwritten notice curling away from a shop window near Omokgyo Station; its loose corner has stuck in his mind. He has tried making a stricter study timetable and telling himself one exam does not decide everything, but neither has eased the trapped feeling.

name: Lim Mi-young
occupation: Owner and sole worker at a clothing alterations shop near Chungju’s bus terminal
topic: Whether Mi-young should keep her alterations shop open after losing customers and falling behind on rent.
core_concern: She is afraid the shop is failing because she has failed, and the shame and pressure have become intense. She has not acted on them and is reluctant to tell anyone, especially if she feels pushed.
background: Mi-young runs her shop alone near Chungju Intercity Bus Terminal. Since the new school term began in March 2026, fewer families have brought in uniform alterations; a nearby uniform seller now handles many adjustments itself. Mi-young put a handwritten sign offering quick repairs in the window and posted in a local KakaoTalk group, but neither brought in much work. She felt embarrassed when she took the sign down. On March 18, her landlord texted that she owes 1.4 million won for two months of shop rent and asked whether she plans to leave when the lease ends on April 30. Mi-young has entered the figures in her order notebook several times but keeps putting off telling her husband the full amount. He knows business is slow and has not pressured her; she fears disappointing him and losing the work that gives her days their shape. Her friend Soon-hee suggested closing before the debt grows, which Mi-young heard as sensible but painful. Now she is alone in the shop, watching the terminal buses pull away through the window. This has become frightening.

name: Kim Min-seo
occupation: Freelance graphic designer creating websites and presentation decks for small businesses, working mostly from her apartment
topic: A freelance website project has turned into unpaid revisions while Min-seo adjusts to living alone after a breakup.
core_concern: She worries that her sadness and exhaustion mean she is failing at ordinary life.
background: On January 31, Min-seo's boyfriend moved out of their one-room apartment in Seongnam. She agreed to keep the lease, though the 780,000-won monthly rent now falls entirely on her. On February 6, a café owner in Jeongja-dong approved the website layout she had made; a week later, he sent a fourth round of changes and asked her to redo the mobile menu before paying the remaining invoice. She replied politely and worked late, then replayed her message, worrying that even her mild mention of the original agreement sounded rude. She tried taking walks to sketch storefront signs and making a one-pan dinner, but returning to the quiet apartment felt harder each time. She has no method or intent. She has left friends' messages unanswered because she fears becoming a burden. On the surface, she is upset about the client and money; underneath, she is exhausted and sad.

name: Park Sang-woo
occupation: Owner of a small print-and-copy shop in Ansan, handling orders, machine maintenance, and deliveries himself
topic: An overdue print order payment and the shop rent due this month.
core_concern: The financial pressure is bringing back feelings he remembers from a dark period in early 2024. He wants to tell someone about the attempt and his recent passive thoughts, but fears a scripted response or an overreaction.
background: In early 2024, during an earlier stretch of business debt, Sang-woo went through a very dark period. His wife knows, but they rarely speak about it. He recovered and kept the shop open. This April, a subcontractor in the Banwol Industrial Complex ordered 2.8 million won of safety-training booklets. Sang-woo stayed late to finish them, but the payment promised for April 30 still has not arrived. On May 8, he called the accounts office twice and was told to wait for approval. He felt angry at having to chase money for work already delivered. The shop rent is due next week, and his wife noticed that he had moved money from their household account to cover paper costs. Their argument ended when their teenage son came home from hagwon. Sang-woo has checked the invoice and delivery receipt again; both are correct. Now the copier's toner light keeps blinking over the counter, and he is dreading another call to the landlord. What frightens him most is how familiar his exhaustion feels. He fears he is slipping back toward that state.

name: Lee Ji-yoon
occupation: Researcher at a Pohang battery-materials company, testing how cathode samples hold up over repeated charging
topic: A troubling result in a cathode cycling test at work.
core_concern: She worries that admitting the spreadsheet mistake will make Han and her coworkers see her as incompetent, but she knows they need the accurate result before the review.
background: On March 9, Ji-yoon noticed that channel 12 in a 200-cycle cathode test showed a sharp capacity drop, while her summary spreadsheet showed a smoother result. She felt uneasy but hoped it was a plotting error. On March 10, she checked the raw log after most coworkers had left and found that she had copied the wrong column into the summary. The raw result still needs to be reviewed; she has not altered or hidden the data. She felt embarrassed, then stayed late remaking graphs instead of writing the routine documentation, which added to her backlog. She drafted a note to senior researcher Han twice and deleted it both times, afraid he would think she cannot be trusted with the tests. A team review is coming up on March 12. At home in Pohang, with an unwashed lab jacket over a chair, she keeps replaying the mistake and privately calls the backlog 'the tide coming in.' She calls it 'not a big deal.'

name: Kim Sun-young
occupation: Insurance planner at an independent agency branch in Goyang, handling health and life policies for local clients
topic: A disputed policy cancellation and pressure to ask clients for referrals.
core_concern: She feels like a bad mother and an incompetent insurance planner.
background: On March 5, a longtime Goyang client cancelled a health policy Sun-young had helped renew. The cancellation will reverse about ₩680,000 in commission. Sun-young checked her call notes twice and believes she explained the renewal terms, but the client says she felt rushed. At the March 9 branch meeting, her manager put referral totals on the whiteboard and asked everyone to bring in five names by Friday. Sun-young felt embarrassed and frightened that colleagues would see her as careless. She tried asking the manager to review the call notes with her; he told her to focus on new business instead. On Sunday, she checked the household payment calendar as usual and saw her daughter's hagwon fee due later in the month. She has not told her husband about the reversal because she expects to cry if she starts. That evening, while rinsing soil from the balcony scallions, she felt overwhelmed. She has not acted on it. She fears being seen as an unfit mother or unreliable colleague.

name: Lim Kyung-hee
occupation: Owner and sole worker of a small clothing alterations shop near Cheonan Station; she is behind on the shop rent
topic: A tiring evening finishing school-uniform alterations.
core_concern: She is afraid she may lose the shop and has hidden how far behind she is on rent from her daughter.
background: In early March 2026, Kyung-hee took several school-uniform hemming orders at her alterations shop near Cheonan Station. She was briefly pleased to have the work, but the small fees did little to ease her worry. She owes 1.36 million won in February and March shop rent. On March 6, her landlord sent a KakaoTalk message asking for payment by March 20; when she asked to pay in installments, he declined. She put a notice about quick alterations in the window, but it has brought in little extra work. Her daughter in Asan wants to visit this weekend, and Kyung-hee has not told her the shop may have to close. She checks the accounts after closing and lies awake, ashamed of needing help and afraid of burdening her daughter. She is distressed. Her dramatic phrases are figures of speech.

name: Park Ji-eun
occupation: farmer who grows lettuce and perilla leaves in a small leased greenhouse outside Uijeongbu
topic: A reduced perilla-leaf order after a difficult greenhouse harvest.
core_concern: She fears her knee will force her to work less, that they cannot afford the lost income, and that she is becoming a burden to her husband.
background: On March 5, 2026, a buyer at Uijeongbu Jeil Market reduced Ji-eun's next perilla-leaf order from 30 bundles to 12 because some leaves had cold-damaged edges. She felt embarrassed but told him she understood. The next morning, her knee hurt badly during the early harvest; condensation dripped from the greenhouse plastic onto her sleeves as she checked the vents and watering lines. She tried harvesting later, but the buyer needed the leaves early. She also considered paid help, then worried the cost would use up what little the crop earned. Her husband noticed her limping and offered to take over a morning, but she said she was fine. Since then, she has spent her usual quiet hour alone without opening her sudoku book or watching baseball highlights. She feels trapped between working through the pain and losing income, and increasingly worries that her husband would have an easier life if she needed less from him. She has not told anyone that part. The lost order has made her feel frightened and burdensome.

name: Lee Ye-eun
occupation: Full-time candidate for the Busan municipal grade-9 administrative civil service exam, studying mainly at a neighborhood study café
topic: A disappointing practice score days before the Busan municipal civil service exam.
core_concern: She feels her exam distress is being brushed aside, and she has ongoing psychiatric care.
background: On June 17, 2025, Ye-eun scored 76 on a Gongdan-gi mock exam, down from 82 the previous week. Her question log shows that most of the lost points came from administrative law, a subject she had thought was improving. With the Busan grade-9 exam on June 21, she spent the next day at her neighborhood study café redoing those questions, but kept rereading the same explanations. At dinner, her mother asked whether she was ready and then quietly put an extra boiled egg beside her rice. Ye-eun felt cared for and ashamed at once: her savings from her old office job are paying for the café, and she cannot bear the thought of another year of studying. She sent a long voice note to a college friend, deleted it before the friend heard it, and tried walking along Oncheoncheon instead. Neither settled her for long. The mock score is the surface problem. She has continued psychiatric care since 2023. Thoughts about not wanting to be here have returned this week, without a current plan or intent. She worries that saying this aloud will frighten her mother or make someone dismiss her exam worries as merely a symptom.

name: Jung Ji-woo
occupation: Part-time barista at a small café near Iksan Station
topic: A mistake on a café closing sheet and an uncomfortable message in the staff KakaoTalk chat.
core_concern: She fears that her manager, mother, and anyone she tells will see her as unreliable or dramatic. Underneath the work worry, things have felt very bad.
background: Ji-woo works part-time at a small café near Iksan Station and lives with her mother while saving money. Since late February, extra shifts have left her exhausted; her room is cluttered, and she keeps postponing a trip to the bank. On March 12, 2026, after covering a coworker’s closing shift, she entered the milk count incorrectly on the closing sheet. The next morning, the manager asked about the discrepancy in the staff KakaoTalk chat. Embarrassed, Ji-woo apologized immediately and offered to cover another shift before anyone asked. The manager replied, 'We’ll check it tomorrow,' which she has reread several times. She tried comparing the delivery slip with her notes, but could not settle her worry. Her mother noticed she was worn out and told her not to take on so much; Ji-woo heard it as another sign that she was disappointing someone. She feels ashamed of the mistake and of how strongly she reacted. She has not told anyone.

name: Park Ha-jun
occupation: Job seeker applying for entry-level shipping administration roles at logistics companies in Busan
topic: A short reply from a recruiter after Ha-jun corrected a job application attachment.
core_concern: He worries the recruiter sees him as careless or bothersome, and he feels ridiculous for worrying about something so small.
background: On May 12, Ha-jun applied through Saramin for an entry-level shipping administration role at a logistics company serving Busan Port. That evening he noticed the attached spreadsheet still had a draft filename. He emailed the corrected file the next morning and received a brief reply: “확인했습니다” (“Confirmed”). He was relieved at first, then began wondering whether sending a correction had made him look careless. His friend Min-su said the reply sounded normal, and a walk along Oncheoncheon helped for a while, but Ha-jun has kept reopening the email alongside his application spreadsheet. When his mother asked about the job over dinner on May 16, he said there was no news.
